speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY UNANSWERED
subtopic: HEALTH OF ANIMALS REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I desire to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) a certain matter of importance in regard to which I shall ask him two questions. For the safeguarding of the health of animals in Canada, certain regulations were passed prohibiting the importation of goods packed in hay or straw-I think fodder is the term generally used-coming from areas in Great Britain or elsewhere infected with the foot and mouth disease. I understand that notice to this effect was given the transportation companies in November, but recently there arrived in Vancouver on one of the Canadian merchant marine ships a cargo, a large portion of which consisted of goods packed in this prohibited material. I am informed that a very substantial part of this cargo has been ordered returned, other portions having been permitted to land. I want to ask two questions:	Is it
not possible to permit the unpacking of these goods under careful supervision, the packing material to be immediately destroyed, and thus avert a loss to the importer who undoubtedly is innocent in the matter? In the second place, why Should local importers be subjected to such loss and inconvenience when the fault rests very largely with the transportation company, in this case with the government merchant marine?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY UNANSWERED
subtopic: HEALTH OF ANIMALS REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The situation complained of
is practically as my hon. friend has stated it, 57
except that additional steps were taken as long ago as August last. The United States government had passed a similar law prohibiting the importation of goods into that country when packed in hay and straw, and as we had a working arrangement with that government whereby we should have regulations of a similar nature with regard to imports from foreign countries, we found it all the more imperative, not only in the interests of Canadian stock but also for the purpose of carrying out our end of the arrangement, to impose this restriction with regard to goods packed in this material coming from countries infected with the foot and mouth disease. However, we allowed goods to come in packed in this way wherever a certificate accompanied them indicating that there was no foot and mouth disease in the exporting country. A number of such shipments came in and we drew the attention of the importers to the fact that this certificate could be obtained from the exporting country. We also extended the time of grace to January 1, hoping that the offenders, who as my hon. friend points out are really the shipping companies and not the innocent importers, might have time to accustom themselves to the regulations. We recognized that we were in the difficult position of being obliged to protect the live stock of the country on the one hand, and, on the other hand, to give as far as possible some consideration to the shipper. So that, as I say, we extended the time to January 1, after which the rule was to be hard-and-fast; and in the meantime we did our best to fumigate and burn all straw coming with such shipments. There was a difficulty, however; we found that shipments of these goods were accumulating at such a rate that it would take an army of officers to fumigate and bum the straw. Finally, therefore, we decided to extend the time to January 15, taking the ground that, after that, under no consideration should the practice be allowed to continue. And we took this ground for several reasons. In the first place, so long as we allowed the goods to land in this kind of packing, the shipping companies apparently would continue to accept such shipments, and the evil would go on in perpetuity. In the second place, we had not a sufficient number of men to take care of all the parcels that were coming in; we could not properly fumigate and dispose of them. And there was a third reason. There is always an element of danger in unpacking these goods, because the moment you begin to fuss with them you increase the opportunities that already exist, for the germs to scatter. At the beginning, we usually destroyed the straw in some of the

Health of Animals

incinerators, but it was inevitable, in the transportation of such goods, that the infection should spread; and for that reason we decided that we should have to stop receiving the goods at this end. If we did not do something of the kind the shipping companies would continue to accept delivery at the other end, and so the danger would persist. Apparently there is a hardship and I do not know how we shall overcome it, but at the same time we must protect our live stock interests. This matter was brought to my attention by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay), and if it can be shown, even yet, that a preference should be given to supplies entering into a government contract, such as the dry dock at Vancouver, I am willing to consider the matter further. The trouble, however, is that if we give a preference to one, even though the goods in that case may be delivered by the Canadian merchant marine, it is difficult indeed to see how we can refuse others. Certainly, so long as we receive goods as we have been receiving them, the shipping companies will continue to accept delivery at the other end.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY UNANSWERED
subtopic: HEALTH OF ANIMALS REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to ask one
other question. Could not some alternative scheme, say at a moderate cost of unpacking and destroying the material, be substituted for the arbitrary order for absolute return, which in many cases will entail very serious losses? Let me illustrate the point without labouring it. I have in mind a company that ordered goods-I am not referring to the dry dock at the moment-upon which they depended to complete a contract within a specified time. As it happens, these goods were not accompanied by the necessary certificate and consequently an order has been issued for their return, so that it may be two or three months before the contractors receive the necessary supplies. The result may be a penalty under the contract. If the minister could provide the alternative of segregating these goods and destroying the fodder, at the cost of the shipper, then at least in an extreme case such as I have mentioned the difficulty might to some extent be overcome. I ask the minister and his colleagues to earnestly consider this in the interests of trade.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY UNANSWERED
subtopic: HEALTH OF ANIMALS REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We have been considering it very carefully, Mr. Speaker, but the element of danger is present. I am in receipt quite recently of a number of telegrams from the western provinces urging me to continue these restrictions and to take no chances of the disease being introduced. The telegrams include one from Premier Bracken

and another from the live stock interests of Alberta. I know it is a hardship to innocent shippers. In my opinion the right course is to prosecute those shipping companies that are landing embargoed goods on our shores.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY UNANSWERED
subtopic: HEALTH OF ANIMALS REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Including the Canadian
Government Merchant Marine?

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY UNANSWERED
subtopic: HEALTH OF ANIMALS REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not see why
action should not be taken against them if they are landing goods on our shores that have been embargoed and prohibited. However, at the urgent request of my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) I will look into the matter further, and if there is any way of doing anything without risk to our live stock industry, and without opening the door to everybody else wanting the same treatment, I shall be delighted to act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I walked into the House this afternoon the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) called my attention to a matter of importance. On the evening of February 28 Ottawa and eastern Canada were visited by a very severe earthquake. As usual, the press reports were very much exaggerated, and Tadoussac, Murray Bay, Baie St. Paul and other north shore towns have been repeatedly . mentioned in the despatches, which inform us that tremors continued for several days after the first shocks and that considerable damage has been done in that part of the country. I know the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has already sent one of his officials to inspect the district, but I think he would be well advised to have an official report made stating exactly what occurred. We do not 57i
want people to imagine that we are in an earthquake belt, but earthquake disturbances may come again, and I think it would be a good thing for the minister to let us know exactly what did take place on the north shore.

speechtext:
1.	Has the government been officially advised that Great Britain has put an embargo on the importation of potaties from Canada into the United Kingdom?
2.	If so, when and why was this embargo put into effect ?
3.	What are the conditions of the embargo?
4.	Was the government advised as to the imminence
f such action on the part of the Imperial governn ent previous to such action being taken?
5.	Was any action taken by the government to attempt to prevent such an embargo being put into effect ?
6.	If such an effort was made on the part of the Canadian government, what was the nature of the representations made to the Imperial government?
7.	Has any effort been made to have these conditions modified ?
8.	Does Great Britain admit potatoes from any European countries ?
9.	Does the government know whether conditions alleged to be the cause for the placing of this embargo against potatoes from Canada exist in European countries from which potatoes are admitted into Great Britain?
10.	Do such conditions prevail in Great Britain or n any part thereof?

Questions
11.	Is the government aware that large quantities of potatoes are in railroad transit in this country, or in store at docks ready to be loaded on ship board ?

13.	Are potatoes originating in the United States of America admitted to Great Britain? If not, why?

subtopic: EMBARGO ON POTATOES
speechtext:
1; Yes.
2.	Notification was received in a despatch from the Secretary of State for the Colonies, dated February 16, that, on account of the presence of the Colorado beetle in Canada, and the possibility of its introduction into the United Kingdom through importations of Canadian potatoes, the importation of potatoes from Canada after February 20, 1925, was prohibited.
3.	The embargo is unconditional.
4.	Yes, but unofficially.
5.	Yes.
6 and 7. When the possibility of the embargo was first reported, the following cable was sent to the High Commissioner:
Unofficially reported here that British ministry contemplate putting embargo on Canadian potatoes because of presence here of Colorado beetle. This beetle has been in Canada for half century and to take objection to it now would be extremely unfortunate and untimely in view of recent action of United Kingdom looking to promotion of inter-empire trade by establishing marketing committee upon which dominions have been invited to appoint representatives. Urge you have any such suggested action stayed until whole situation is carefully surveyed from all angles as another ill advised cattle embargo incident would be unfortunate.
The following is a quotation from a letter addressed by the High Commissioner to the Right Honourable Lord Bledisloe, Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries:
I am enclosing a little article which appeared in the Manchester edition of the Daily Mail yesterday headed "U.S.A. Bacon."
You will notice in the last paragraph of this an allusion to potatoes, in case American potatoes should find their way via Canada to this country. As a matter of fact this would be commercially impossible because the duty on potatoes from the United States to Canada is thirty-five cents per 100 pounds and the United States market is always higher than the Canadian, even in times of plenty like the present year, and if they went through Canada in bond they would be bound to be marked U.S.A. potatoes.
You are probably well aware of the care taken in grading and marketing Canadian potatoes. They are run over wire screens for sizes, then bagged, and each bag must have a tag attached by a government inspector, marked "Canadian A", and "Canadian B" or "Canadian C." I may add that the potatoes are examined by two government inspectors-by the original grader and the potato health inspector at the point of shipment.
The information I get is that it is practically an impossibility for the Colorado beetle to appear in any Canadian tuber because, as you know, the slugs feed on the leaf and then bury themselves in the earth, not in the tuber, and the tuber being run over wire screens for sizes and then run again over hand racks
at the point of shipment precludes any possibility of them containing anything that might develop into a Colorado beetle.
These representations were, however, unsuccessful and the embargo was placed on Canadian potatoes. The government was, however, successful in inducing the British government to except from the conditions of the embargo any Canadian potatoes afloat at the time the embargo was put into effect.
A further attempt was made to have the restrictions removed1 the following cable having been sent to the British ministry.
The Entomological branch of the Department of Agriculture has just completed a close biological study of the Colorado beetle and from their study of the habits of the insect, there would appear to be no danger whatever of the beetle being transported in shipments of potatoes exported from Canada.
The Colorado potato beetle in eastern Canada disappears from the plants by the end of September and enters the ground for hibernation. In fact, the large majority of the beetles are in the ground a month earlier. Potatoes exported from Canada to England are dug in October, at which time, as stated, the beetles are inactive, being m hibernation in the ground. After digging, the potatoes are machine-graded before shipment and the danger that any beetles could remain in association with the potatoes through all this process is infinitesimal.
Our officers who have made special observations of this insect have never reported the finding of the beetles in bags, barrels, or other containers in which potatoes are shipped.
During the summer months when the beetles are active, there is a possibility of their being transported with any cargo, but it seems almost inconceivable that the beetles could be introduced with shipments of potatoes which are invariably dug after the beetles have entered the ground for hibernation.
We have no records, nor know of no cases in other countries of the insect having been distributed through shipments of potatoes.
As the department has an established potato inspection service, Canada would suggest that the Imperial government accept shipments of potatoes from this country subject to their being accompanied by certificates as to freedom from Colorado potato beetle due to having undergone such grading and inspection as would permit of such guarantee.
No reply to this has yet been received.
8.	Yes.
9.	Yes, the Colorado beetle is found in the Bordeaux district in France, but importations from this district are forbidden, while importations from other parts of France must be accompanied by a certificate to the effect that the Colorado beetle is non-existent in the export district.
10.	The information supplied by the British Ministry is to the contrary.
11.	Replies received from railway companies and the principal shippers would indicate that practically few cars were en route when the embargo went into effect, and all these were immediately diverted to other markets on news of the embargo being received.

12.	Answered by No. 11.
13.	No. For the same reason that Canadian importations are prohibited, namely, the presence of the Colorado beetle in the United States.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ELEVATOR SCREENINGS
GOVERNMENT ELEVATOR SCREENINGS
speechtext: Under what terms and conditions are screenings disposed of at the Dominion government elevators at Calgary and Edmonton?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ELEVATOR SCREENINGS
speechtext:
The majority of the screenings from grain received at the Canadian government elevators at Calgary and Edmonton are not the property of the elevator as they are removed from wheat carrying a dockage amounting to 3 per cent or over, and coarse grains 5 per cent or over, and, therefore, belong to the owners of the grain. Warehouse receipts are issued for these screenings and the screenings are shipped upon instructions of the owners and the surrender of the warehouse receipts. The elevators have absolutely no control over the disposition of these screenings.
In the case of screenings which accrue to the elevator in lieu of cleaning charges, that is, screenings from Wheat carrying less than 3 per cent dockage and coarse grains carrying less than 5 per cent dockage, they are practically all disposed of to stock feeders in the two cities named at current market prices.
No contracts or agreements are entered into for the sale of these screenings. They are sold whenever available to any parties desirous of purchasing, preference being given to farmers and stock feeders.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW

speechtext:
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Senate as at present appointed and constituted is not of the greatest advantage to Canada.
He said': Mr. Speaker, I make no apology in proposing this resolution. I realize fully that many experienced parliamentarians will look askance at, perhaps resent, the huimble effort of one so unexperienced as myself in proposing this problem for the consideration of the House. But I think my defence, and an ample one, is to be found in the fact that public opinion has pressed this long standing question to the very gates of parliament itself; and if, perchance, as & result of the discussion of this resolution the subject of Senate reform is pushed just a little bit closer toward a satisfactory solution, then I shall! indeed hive had ample compensation. I am not unmindful either that a similar resolution, perhaps similarly worded, might, with some justification, 'be introduced by an energetic member of the other chamber and having special
application to this House, because in what I have to say with regard to whatever shortcomings there are, in my humble judgment, in connection with the operation and constitution of the Senate, I do not forget that this chamber likewise has some shortcomings.
In preparing a resolution of this character two courses presented themselves to my mind: First, I could have prepared in definite form my own convictions of the proper method to take to effect Senate reformation. I have, however, to some extent profited by the experience of the past in that regard, because similar definite resolutions, presented not only in this House but in the other chamber, have been fruitless of results. The second method is the one which I have adopted-the method of proposing a resolution which allowing the greatest latitude for discussion, and the fullest opportunity for the presentation of any plans of reformation, yet does give this House the opportunity, if it so desires, to express what it has never done before-its opinion as to whether or not it is satisfied with the constitution of the Senate as it at present exists. May I say that a further consideration moved me to some extent, and that was by reason of what I had anticipated would be the course taken by the government, in the statements at least of the Prime Minister, of an intention to introduce some measure of Senate reform. I anticipated that government action would be initiated by calling a provincial conference-that would be the initial step in the programme,-and it occurred to me that perhaps the provincial conference foreshadowed in the Speech from the Throne would inquire as to what the attitude of this House was-whether or not we are satisfied- and, further, it occurred to me that the best thing to do would be to take this first step- to ascertain whether or not the House of Commons is satisfied with the Senate as at present constituted. May I say also at the outset, that to my mind no question requires a clearer insight into our constitution, no question calls for a clearer analysis of our institutions, and certainly none should command in larger measure moderation in statement and in presentation.
When one thinks of the genesis of our parliamentary institutions in Canada we immediately thrust our minds back to the British North America Act, because that is, at least, the statutory enactment which provides for this parliament. The British North America Act of 1867 provided for a parliament composed of two bodies; the Commons, the lower chamber, elected by popular vote; the Senate, the upper house, nominated for life by the
The Senate

Governor General in Council. So far as the British North America Act is concerned there
is only one provision which in any way limits the power of the Senate, and that is a provision which declares that money bills shall originate in the House of Commons. Therefore, I think one is legally correct in stating that the powers of the Senate and the powers of the House of Commons are not only coequal but co-extensive, with the single exception that I have mentioned.
Now, in framing the constitution which we have to-day what motives animated the Fathers of Confederation, what models had they before them, if any, to copy? There were two possible schemes for confederation: One was a legislative union, the other was a federal union. I think some of the Fathers of Confederation would have preferred a legislative union, but they were animated by the example and guided by the model which was furnished to them by our great neighbours to the south. Many of them, including Sir John A. Macdonald, frankly confessed their admiration of that constitution. They had not only the constitution itself before them, but they had the benefit of the long experience the people of the United States had had with that constitution. They observed how that constitution had served at a time when the population of the United States was less than two million people, when its inhabited area amounted to something like one hundred thousand square miles. They had observed how that constitution had fitted the desires and ambitions of that great country, even at the time when its population had increased to something over thirty-five million and its inhabited area extended to almost three million square miles. In addition to that they had observed the great political, economic and social changes which had taken place during that experiment in legislation, and they had undoubtedly admired the pliability of the constitution to meet these changing and changed conditions. Moreover, they had before them the experience of that constitution, under period of the greatest stress, the period of the American Civil War, and they had observed too that even states whioh desired to secede from the union had adopted for their confederacy a scheme almost identical with that embodied in the federal constitution. So it was not unnatural, with conditions not altogether dissimilar, that the Fathers of Confederation should have looked with admiring eyes and adopted as far as practicable the principles embodied in the American constitution.
But you will at once say "Why dad they not adopt the elective principle as applicable

to the second chamber, that principle being adopted in the American constitution?" I need not remind the House that at the time of confederation some of the confederating provinces had elective legislative councils. The Maritime provinces had not. It was I think largely as a matter of compromise that the nominative life principle was adopted. There was much criticism of it. I remember very well reading about objections raised by such statesmen as Sir Oliver Mowat to the adoption of the nominative life principle, and I remember very well too that some of those who gave their assent to that principle subsequently recanted, and I include in this number Hon. George Brown and Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, subsequently Prime Minister of this country. Both those distinguished gentlemen subsequently recanted their allegiance to the nominative life principle and therefore I say that the adoption of the nom-4 p.m. inative life principle for our Senate came largely as the result of compromise. I do not think that it was considered such a serious matter, and many who were engaged in that important enterprise of drafting a constitution for this country were forced to give way on this principle in order to secure harmony on other more important
principles.
That being so, the United States model being the one we adopted, paying however due allegiance to the monarchical system of government, what, I ask you, might reasonably be expected of a Senate, and what duties might it reasonably be called upon to perform? What was expected of the United States Senate? In that connection, let me quote the words of the chief architect of the United States constitution, Alexander Hamilton, showing what he anticipated would be the purpose of the Senate and what duties it should be called upon to perform. He said:
First. It is a misfortune incident to republican government, though in a less degree than to other governments, that those who administer it, may forget their obligations to their constituents, and prove unfaithful to their important trust. In this point of view, a senate, as a second branch of the legislative assembly, distinct from, and dividing the power with, a first, must be in all cases a salutary check on the government. It doubles the security to the people, by requiring the concurrence of two distinct bodies in schemes of usurpation or perfidy, where the ambition or corruption of one would otherwise be sufficient. This is a precaution founded on such clear principles, and now so well understood in the United States, that it would be more than superfluous to enlarge on it. I will barely remark, that, as the improbability of sinister combinations will be in proportion to the dissimilarity in the genius of the two bodies, it must be politic to distinguish them from each other by every circumstance which will consist with a due harmony in all proper measures, and with the genuine principles of republican government.

The Senate
Second. The necessity of a senate is not less indicated by the propensity of all single and numerous assemblies, to yield to the impulse of sudden and violent passions, and to be seduced by factious leaders into intemperate and pernicious resolutions. Examples on this subject might be cited without number; and from proceedings within the United States, as well as from the history of other nations. But a position that will not be contradicted, need not be proved. All that need be remarked, is, that a body which is to correct this infirmity, ought itself to be free from it, and consequently ought to be less numerous. It ought moreover to possess great firmness, and consequently ought to hold its authority by a tenure of considerable duration.
Third. Another defect to be supplied by a senate, lies in a want of due acquaintance with the objects and principles of legislation. It is not possible that an assembly of men, called for the most part, from pursuits of a private nature, continued in appointment for a short time, and led by no permanent motive to devote the intervals of public occupation to a study of the laws, the affairs, and the comprehensive interests of their country, should, if left wholly to themselves, escape a variety of important errors in the exercise of their legislative trust.
In amplifying this third point he mentions one or two 'things which have frequently been quoted, and1 which I desire to quote now. He said:
A good government implies two things; first, fidelity to the object of government, which is the happiness of the people; secondly, a knowledge of the means by which that object can be best attained. Some governments are deficient in both these qualities: Most governments are deficient in the first. I scruple not to assert, that, in the American governments, too little attention has been paid to the last. The federal constitution avoids this error; and what merits particular notice, it provides for the last in a mode which increases the security for the first.
The fourth purpose which Alexander Hamilton says the Senate serves is as follows:
Fourth. The mutability in the public councils, arising from a rapid succession of new members, however qualified they may be, points out in the strongest manner, the necessity of some stable institution in the government. Every new election in the states, is found to change one half of the representatives. From this change of men must proceed a change of opinions; and from a change of opinions, a change of measures. But a continual change even of good measures is inconsistent with every rule of prudence, and every prospect of success.
The fifth purpose he gave as folfows:
A fifth desideratum, illustrating the utility of a senate, is the want of a due sense of national character. Without a select and stable member of the government, the esteem of foreign powers will not only be forfeited by an unenlightened and variable policy, proceeding from the causes already mentioned; but the national councils will not possess that sensibility to the opinion of the world, which is perhaps not less necessary in order to merit, than it is to obtain, its respect and confidence.
And finally as a sixth reason for the Senate, he paints out the want in some important cases of a due responsibility in the government to the people, arising from that frequency of elections, which in other cases produces this responsibility. He proceeds:
The remark will, perhaps, appear not only new, but paradoxical. It must nevertheless be acknowledged, when explained, to be as undeniable as it is important.
Responsibility, in order to be reasonable, must be limited to objects within the power of the responsible party; and in order to be effectual, must relate to operations of that power, of which a ready and proper judgment can be formed by the constituents. The objects of government may be divided into two general classes; the one depending on measures, which have singly an immediate and sensible operation, the other depending on a succession of well chosen and well connected measures, which have a gradual and perhaps unobserved operation.
It is -unnecessary to point out the significance of the sixth purpose enunciated' by the distinguished author. Shortly, as I understand the chief purpose of the Senate, it is to put a check upon democratic intensity, if I may use that term. It purposes to set against the caution and experience of age the inexperience and the zeal of youth. I have considerable sympathy with these purposes, but I think sometimes that we may forget that since these principles have been written a hundred years of history have also been written, and I am not so sure now that, instead of trying to curtail democratic intensity, we might more properly be engaged in this case in trying to curtail reaction. In our day the reactionary has full and complete opportunity for his activities, whereas the man who seeks even the slightest measure of reform finds himself opposed by all kinds of checks and balances. After all, however, these checks and balances, I take it, cannot stem the tide. It may be well, that the tide of democracy should be somewhat delayed, but it must move on. There is another and important consideration pointed out by Hamilton in another place in his work, which is essential in a federal system of government and which gives special significance to a second chamber, namely, the necessity of preserving unimpaired and intact the sovereignty remaining in the states or local divisions and the necessity of preserving the established rights of sections and minorities. These things are fundamental in a federal system, and their preservation is the especial obligation of a Senate, these its special task.
Having these various principles in mind, I want to deal now shortly with the Canadian Senate, and I think that probably I shall be on ground which is not objectionable, at any rate to any great extent. What defects are there in the Senate as it is at present constituted and as it operates at the present time? In how far does it diverge from the original principles which brought it into being? These are questions which I shall now address to the House. First of all, I desire to indicate what I regard as the defects of constitution, if I may
The Senate

use that term. In my judgment there are at least three. The appointment of the Senate by the central authority, the Governor General in Council, is absolutely inconsistent with the federal system of government. The members of that body are appointed by the Governor General in Council supposedly for the purpose of conserving provincial rights and sectional interests. But they are not responsible to the people of those sections or provinces; they are not responsible to the provincial legislatures. Neither the people nor the legislature in any province have any right whatsoever in the appointment of the particular individuals who are supposed, theoretically at least, to conserve their special interests. I say therefore that the appointment by the Governor General in Council of the individuals who constitute the Senate is thoroughly inconsistent with the federal system of government. There is nothing new in that observation, for I would call the attention of the House to the fact that as long ago as 1874 the Hon. David Mills, afterwards Minister of Justice under Sir Wilfrid Laurier's regime, brought in a resolution based on that very inconsistency and asked the House to go into committee of the Whole to consider his remedial proposals. The House, by a vote of 77 to 74, concurred in his view and went into committee of the Whole; but so far as the records show, no further action was taken. That is the first point with regard to the Senate.
Let me ask at. this juncture whether in aE its history, in all the story of its life from eonfedteration up to the present day, anyone can indicate any case in which the Senate has stood1 for the protection of provincial rights, for the protection of sectional interests, for the protection of minority rights? I know of no such ease myself, although I admit that I am liable to err. I have examined! with care a book written by one of the chief proponents of the Senate as it is at present constituted, and from cover to cover of that book I have been unable to find a single instance in which the Senate has in any special way shown a desire to carry out the fundamental purpose for which it was created. And' surely there have been ample opportunities for the exercise of that prerogative. Surely no one as he sees this Dominion to-day would admit for a moment that there has not been ample opportunity to have prevented, or at least allayed, this sectional discord1 which is characteristic of almost all parts of the country. Surely there have been ample opportunities to conserve provincial rights. I recall that Sir Oliver Mowat had a very prolonged struggle with the government of Sir John A.
[Mr. Shaw.J
Macdonald in his effort to conserve the rights of the province of Ontario.
The next objection I have to the constitution of the Senate is that the appointment for life is undemocratic. I need' only mention that point to convince hon. gentlemen of its truth. But the difficulty is-I will put it no stronger-that appointment for life is apt to make the occupants of that chamber lose all initiative; it is apt in some cases, I trust in very few, to create an indifference on the part of the senators to their duties. After all, I wonder what it is that inspires the hon. members of this House to action, and keeps them alert and vigorous in the particular task for which they were chosen? What is it? It is simply the desire, the quite proper desire, to merit the continued esteem of those who are responsible for their presence here.
My next objection to the Senate is that it is altogether too large from the standpoint of numbers. The United States Senate, which was to some extent the model for our federal institution, has a membership approximately the same as that of the Senate of Canada. And the Senate of that great country is called1 upon to protect the sectional interests of something like 110.000,000 people. Surely no one would deny that it effectively performs its task. So I say that the Senate of Canada today is altogether too large. I believe too that the Senate should be proportioned equally as between the various provinces. Let me illustrate. Under our constitution, the province from which I Come is entitled to 6 senators while the province of Ontario is entitled to 24. It may be that in a very few years, although perhaps not in my lifetime, the province of Alberta may surpass in population the province of Ontario, for i't has made far (greater proportionate progress in the last twenty years. Would it then ibe right and proper and fair that t'he present disproportion should continue in (the respective representations in the Senate, although the population might have changed very considerably? It does occur to me that, designed as this body is for the protection of provincial rights, and the conservation of special and sectional interests, the representation might fairly be proportioned equally so far as the various provinces are concerned. These are substantially what I find to be the main defects, if I may use that term, in the Senate constitution.
I want now to deal with what I think are some of the defects in its operation. Mind you, I am not complaining about any particular members of that body; in whatever I say I am not blaming them 'but thie system which has madte the present situation possible. First of all, let me say that the Senate

The Senate
as it is constituted is partisan and not in-dependtent. I do not have to rely on my own judgment in that matter, but I aim sure that it must appeal to everyone that such is the case. Is it not natural that the recipient of a place in that chamber should feel himself owing some allegiance to* those who are responsible for his appointment? Even one of the hon. members of that 'body some years ago in agreeing with that view stated that if Sir John A. Macdonald-who had appointed him to that high position-should aak him as a favour to vote in a certain wiay on a ipai'-ticular measure, he would feel under some obligation to db so, because he said, "I am in the position of a delegate in the presence of the delegator."
It will no doubt be interesting to hon. members if at this stage I read the judgment of a distinguished observer of parliamentary institutions in all parts of the world; I refer to the late Viscount Bryce. He says in Modern Democracies:
The plan of nomination by the executive is even less to be commended, because members seem to be usually selected for party reasons;
I doubt if any one here would seriously controvert that statement.
Sometimes, as in Canada, not merely for the sake of securing for the ministry a majority in the second chamber but also in order to reward its elderly supporters, who, weary of courting constituencies, gladly subside into a dignified armchair. There are countries in which secretly rendered political services or liberal contributions to party funds are believed to open the door of the chamber to those whose merits the public had failed to discover.
That is the opinion of a distinguished observer. But when one comes to look at the political composition of the Senate itself, one finds how this pernicious patronage system has exacted its full toll of the independence of that body. I hold in my hand a statement showing the political membership by provinces of the Senate in 1896, the year in *which the Liberals came into power. There were then 13 Liberals and 68 Conservatives, with one seat vacant. The House of Commons at the same time was composed of 117 Liberals and 89 Conservatives. - Surely no one would suggest for a moment that the Senate represented the political views of the country at large. The next change of government took place in 1911, when the situation was almost completely reversed, there being then in the Senate 66 Liberals and 20 Conservatives, whereas in the election of that year 133 Conservatives and only 86 Liberals were returned to the House of Commons. In 1917, the year of the advent of Union government, the situation had again been changed, there being 40 Liberals and 46 Conservative senators.

So I suggest that in operation the Senate is a partisan body; it is not independent. I do not mean totally independent of the public will, but not likely to bring to the consideration of every question a fair and impartial judgment, unfettered by partisan considerations and uninfluenced by party affiliations, with the courage to face unpopularity in its decisions. In this respect the Senate has failed. Moreover when the Senate is of the same political complexion as the party in power, it is largely a useless body, except for revising purposes, and I suggest that such revision can be done in a far more effective and adequate way. When the Senate is of an opposite complexion to the party in power then it becomes in most cases a real hindrance to effective government, resulting sometimes in near legislative paralysis.
My next complaint is that the Senate does not reflect the varied national life of this country. I do not say, mind you, that the House of Commons does either. But it is natural to suppose that most hon. members secure their right to occupy a seat in the Senate by reason of attendance in this House or association with it, and the result is that, generally speaking, they are not representative of the various sections of our national life. Viscount Bryce in his Modern Democracies also points out that a senate to be really effective must represent all the main currents of our industrial, commercial and social life-agriculture, commerce, manufacturing, and so on. I do not think anyone who has given consideration to the subject would contend for a single moment that the political method of appointment conduces to a fair representation in the Senate of our national life.
Another objection which I would urge is that the Senate sits and awaits action by this House. We have an illustration of it at present; the Senate is waiting for what may fall from the table of the House of Commons in order to amend or change it. Now, charged as the Senate is under our federal system with high and important functions, surely there is ample opportunity for that body to engage its time profitably at this juncture when the whole country is being devitalized by sectional differences and when serious industrial strife is threatened. Surely the Senate might by a careful study of our economic, social and industrial life, assist materially in solving the problems that now confront the Dominion.
Lastly, if you put the Senate on its lowest possible basis, that of a revising chamber alone, then I say it does not even discharge that duty adequately, because in the concluding stages of the session it is showered
n\lr. Slmw.]
with a host of bills from this House, and it must either throw them out or pass them with scant opportunity to give them careful consideration and intelligent revision. So on that basis alone I submit that the Senate is not an efficient revising body.
Now, I could quote Viscount Bryce, a very keen observer of constitutions, to the effect that the Senate of Canada is one of tlie weakest second chambers of its character in existence. That is the considered statement of that distinguished gentleman some two or three years ago in his book, Modern Democracies.

the quotation to which I refer at page 441, volume 2 of Modern Democracies. In dealing with the various kinds of chambers he mentions those in the same category, and he says:
Amongst these the French Senate is the strongest and that of Canada the weakest.
I want to read the considered statement of a Canadian author, himself a very astute and keen observer of parliamentary government in this country. I refer to Professor Wrong of the University of Toronto. He says:
It is not a body that occupies an important place in the thought of the Canadian people.
He goes on to amplify that statement; I am not concerned at the moment in reading that part of it. But he'says further:
Always the senators have obeyed the mandate of party; there is no case on record in which a majority in the Senate has opposed, on an important measure, a majority of the same party in the House of Commons. Those who know what is going on at Ottawa admit freely that the Senate does useful work on non-party lines in improving bills; but they will add that it discharges no other useful function.
I see that Professor Wrong and myself disagree on one small particular in connection with that. Summing up his conclusions with regard to the Senate, Professor Wrong says:
1.	The Senate plays a minor part in the political life of Canada, and commands but little authority.
2.	The Senate becomes important only at the time of a change of government in Canada, and its influence is then likely to be used to hamper the new government.
3.	The Senate discharges useful functions in improving the details of the bills sent to it from the House
of Commons.
4.	Experience in Canada has shown that the method of appointment for life works better than would appointment for a term of years.

The Senate
Then he goes on to amplify that view.
The longest term of years to be proposed would probably not exceed seven or eight. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power in Canada for sixteen years. Had the terms of senators expired after even ten years, every Conservative senator would have been replaced by a Liberal during Sir Wilfrid Laurier's tenure of office, and the Senate would have contained only Liberals, a reductio ad absurd urn.
5.	In Canada the tyranny of party has been complete in regard to the Senate. But for this, more men conspicuous in the world of commerce, of letters, of education, might have found a place in the Senate and might have softened the rule of mediocrity which now prevails in the representative institutions of the New World. The party leaders, however, have willed it otherwise, and they have had their way.
But Mr. Speaker, I do not need to rely upon the judgment even of the distinguished authors I have quoted; I can refer the matter to the Senate itself. Some fifteen or twenty years ago-to be exact, in the year 1909-a distinguished gentleman who played a very large part ini the inauguration of this confederation and who lived through all its adversities and many of its changes of parties, himself introduced a resolution in that chamber designed to rectify many of what he thought to be existing evils, and to impart to that body a measure of additional strength. Among other things, he sought to make membership in the Senate partly elective. I refer to a gentleman with almost forty years' experience in that chamber, the late Sir Richard Scott.
Now, if there exist the constitutional defects as well as the defects in the exercise of its functions that I have pointed out, the next question naturally arises, what remedies are available? I must say at the outset that I have no desire in any way to criticize the government for the preliminary action it has taken in connection with this matter. I think that is essential; I think that is necessary under the constitution. But I want to look beyond that; I simply want to suggest that I have in mind the preliminary steps- I do not want the members of the House to get the idea that I would ignore the necessary preliminaries toward effective action.
There are three possible ways to meet this situation: First, abolition; secondly, strengthen the chamber; thirdly, weaken it. With regard to the first, abolition is becoming increasingly popular. It is becoming increasingly popular, I am convinced, because people have not before them any other effective scheme, or any scheme which premises change or reform so far as the Senate is concerned. It arises largely because of the paucity of other schemes, and not because it is the best remedy. The advocates of abolition urge that the Senate is a drag upon democracy; that it is an intrenehment of
special and privileged interests, and that any institution which is based upon a distrust of democracy is necessarily weak and should not be continued. Now, these advocates of abolition apply their theory equally to any scheme of government, be it the unitary system or the federal system. In that particular I think they are perhaps mistaken.
I see no objection to applying the principle of abolition to a unitary form of government but when it comes to a federal form of government with a second chamber charged with the specific duties and obligations which I have mentioned, then I think it would be a mistake to insist on abolition. If abolition is to be the remedy, what organization, what institution, will preserve provincial rights under our system of government? What institution will preserve sectional rights? What institution will there be to preserve the established rights of minorities? Besides, I am not so sure that where a popular chamber is so engrossed in partisan controversy from time to time it has that judicial calm which is essential to the proper and expeditious disposal of all legislation. In addition to that, the chamber-our chamber for example -has not the opportunity for the social and economic study that is essential to the proper solution of many of our problems. However, the abolitionist says, in the words of that English publicist in the late eighties, " Either mend it or end it ".
One other way of going about this matter is to make the Senate stronger, to cure its defects, to add strength to it. Several plans have been suggested; I propose to suggest only one or two, and that very briefly.
One suggestion is to make the Senate elective, to make it responsible to the people whose interests it is supposed to conserve and to preserve-to let the provinces themselves -the ones who are vitally interested, undertake the election of senators. By doing that you add strength to the Senate, because if there is strength in this elective chamber there will likewise be strength in an elective second chamber. The difficulty pointed out by most writers on the subject is the likelihood of deadlock between the two chambers, but with the experience of recent years- Australia, South Africa, Ireland-surely the people of this country should be able to fashion some system that will enable us to untangle readily any deadlocks that may occur.

There are one or two methods based upon the nominative plan to which I want to refer. The first was proposed by a distinguished member of this House. I think because of that alone it is entitled to our serious consideration. The other reason which I think entitles it to our consideration is that it certainly is a thought provoking scheme. I refer to th3 plan proposed in this House some two years ago by the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, whose illness and consequent absence from this House I am sure we all deplore. This distinguished gentleman, after forty years of parliamentary experience in this country, proposed that all the senators should hold office by nomination, that half of them should be appointed by the federal government, and the remaining half be appointed by the legislative assemblies of the various provinces. One can readily see that that plan would be an improvement, upon our present system. But the right hon. gentleman only pays a sort of half allegiance to the principle of provincial rights. That would be the objection I would see to such a plan as that. If it is necessary that state rights should be preserved, if this federal part of our institutions is to be preserved, then the Senate should be chosen entirely by the provinces themselves. Mr. Fielding did not propose that the tenure of the present senators should be changed. His scheme would come into gradual operation, until in course of time it became fully complete.
There is also another very valuable suggestion made by Viscount Bryce. He suggests that life tenure should be eliminated. I do not mean to give the impression that this scheme of his was proposed for Canada alone. He suggests that life tenure should be abolished, that the senators should be selected for a term of years; but his method of selection is to be entirely different from the method now followed or from any of the other proposed methods. A committee of selection is to be set up by both chambers, in our case by both the Commons and the Senate, and this committee of selection is to recommend to these two bodies a list of men distinguished in

civil life who have taken a large part in the national life of the country, or who have done honour to the nation in any way. That is his scheme for creating a second chamber, a second chamber which he limits very greatly so far as its powers are concerned.
I have referred to two methods-to the method of abolition, and the method of strengthening. I now want to refer to the third method, and that is to reduce the Senate powers as they already exist. I said at the outset that the powers of the Senate except in money matters are co-equal and co-extensive with those of the Commons. They have the widest power of initiation in measures of reform, but I think I am fair in saying that they have seldom taken advantage of this power. Now the suggestion along this line is to dilute, if you like, the veto power which now exists. The Senate now have an absolute veto power. Dilute that power until it becomes either a suspensory or a temporary power of veto. That is the plan that is followed in England. Such a scheme will reduce the Senate to comparative impotence. In connection with the English scheme, if hon. gentlemen will read the Parliament Act of 1911, they will observe there one or two very interesting things. First of all, the act itself in its preamble clearly indicates that the veto measure there taken, that is, the effort to make the absolute veto of the House of Lords a mere temporary veto, was only a preliminary step. The second and further step was to create a popular House of Lords. I will read the preamble for the information of hon. members:
Whereas it is intended to substitute for the House of Lords as it at present exists a second chamber constituted on a popular instead of hereditary basis, but such substitution cannot be immediately brought into operation-

The ex-Prime Minister of England, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, has an idea also in connection with Senate reform. He wants to reduce the Senate to a revising chamber, and a revising chamber only. He suggests that it be lessened in number, that it consist entirely of law lords and parliamentary legal draftsmen, and that this body have power, not to change principles at all, but simply to improve the technique of legislation. These are, in short, some of the many schemes which are proposed for Senate reform. The question, after all, it seems to me, comes down to this, as indicated by one writer on the subject: "Do you want an elder brother who is going to advise, who is going to suggest, who is, if necessary, going to check his rash brother, or do you want merely a clerk who will simply cross the t's and dot the i's?"
May I suggest the following as the line that occurs to me along which we may safely travel? I believe, in the first place, that the Senate should be elected; I believe it should be elected by the provinces. If, however, any province should desire a different method of election, or desire the appointment of senators by the legislative assembly, if the majority of them should desire that and they are all prepared to accept it, I have no objection to that. But first of all, make the Senate, either by election or by provincial nomination, responsible to the people whose interests they are called upon to serve. I think also they should be reduced in number. If we had say 36 senators instead of 96, four from each province, if we could claim the services of distinguished men, I think that number would give a fair and adequate representation in that chamber. Then I think they should be chosen for a period of eight years, one half retiring every four years.

Now, Mr. Speaker, may I just say this in conclusion: I have sought to ascertain what principles should govern us in the creation of

I suggest only in outline my own ideas; not that they have any particular value. I simply want to point out in conclusion that our Confederation Act was framed almost sixty years ago. There have been great changes since that time. Even differing theories on government, and on organization, have been propounded. All these are more or less in the melting pot, and have passed through various stages of development. Since that time too, our whole political, social, and industrial fabric has been almost totally changed, and so these rapidly evolving conditions necessitate that we should give some consideration to the institutions which are functioning for the purpose of .preserving and vitalizing our social, industrial, political and economic fabric.
We are not. without some very valuable illustrations as a result of that sixt}' years of experience. May I just suggest some of the things that have happened. The House of Lords in that period has been reduced to comparative impotence. New Zealand with a life tenure for its legislative council has found it necessary to reduce that tenure to a period of seven years. Australia in the interim has adopted an elective system for its Senate. South Africa has adopted a partly elective Senate, with safeguards in the case of a dead-lock which merit our very serious consideration. France prior to 1884 had a life tenure for her Senate. In that year it was changed to an elective system-elected not directly by the people but by the representatives of the various local departments. Since that time too new governments have sprung up. The war created many in Europe. In some of them where the people were homogeneous, where there were not great geographical barriers, where there was not a vast difference in race and creed, they have satisfied themselves with only one assembly. I refer to the states of Latvia and Esthonia. Other countries such as Czecho-Slovakia and Poland, where there were divergencies in these matters, have adopted the federal system, and in each case have provided for an elective Senate. In addition to that we have a most illuminating experience from the country of my hon. friend the member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), a part of the British Empire which furnishes one of the most striking illustrations as to how a second chamber may profitably be constituted. The Irish Free State has a Senate of some sixty members.

The Senate
elected for a term of twelve years. The act under which it is constituted provides that the senators must be citizens who have done honour to the nation by reason of useful public services, or who represent important aspects of the nation's life. One-fourth of the members are chosen by the electors for three years from a panel selected by the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. The Senate and the Chamber of Deputies choose a panel consisting of three times as many names as are to be elected, and these names are then presented to the public for their selection. In that constitution legislative authority in respect to money bills is reserved for the Chamber of Deputies alone. The Senate, however, is empowered to make recommendations. Other bills must be passed or accepted by both houses, but if the Senate does not pass a bill within two hundred and seventy days, or other longer agreed period, after it has been sent to the Senate by the Chamber of Deputies, the bill shall be deemed to have passed both houses in the form in which it last passed the chamber. The Senate, however, may demand a joint sitting of the two houses to debate, but not vote upon a money bill.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these are all the observations I have to make and in conclusion I desire to make a quotation.

I

I come from the province of Ontario, where this matter of Senate reform has occupied the minds of the people to a very large extent and has become a public and practical question. Reading the press of Ontario, and mingling with the people of that province, we find that there is a strong demand for the abolition of the Senate. The fact that the question of Senate reform occupies the attention of the people to a large extent is evidenced by the fact that it has been discussed many times in this House, and through all that discussion there has been a unanimous declaration in favour of some kind of reform, 'but apparently, the difficulty has been to arrive at some conclusion as to the nature of that reform. I hare taken the trouble to go into some of these debates, and through them all I find a general agreement that reform is necessary, and I also find that the great Obstacle in the way of bringing aibout a reform is the fact that no two people are able to agree as to what the nature of that reform should be. The fact is that you cannot find any individual who can propose a reform which will produce the benefits which that individual expected would result. As an instance of that, may I quote from the remarks of the Rigjhit Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the difficulties which 'he saw in the way of reforming the Senate. Speaking on a resolution introduced during the session of 1906, he used these words:	[DOT]
Well, what would be the nature of a reform which would be acceptable to all? This is a question which has puzzled more than one. My hon. friends, the mover and seconder of the resolution, both referred to the convention of 1893, which was held in this city, and in which the reform of the Senate was declared necessary; but while we made that affirmation, the difficulty has always been to settle practically what reform would be acceptable. At once we were met, when we thought of reducing the idea to legislation-and it is a subject which has more than once perplexed the present advisers of His Excellency- with the difficulty of agreeing upon such reform as would be satisfactory to all.
So we find all down through the discussion the main difficulty is to arrive at some method of reform which would be satisfactory to all sections of the country. Because of that difficulty no progress has been made so far. I fMr. Shaw.]
thoroughly agree with the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from West Calgary, but as I have already stated, its fault, if it has any, is that it does not go far enough. I shall therefore move an amendment which I hope w ill meet with the approval of the House and which at least goes some little distance further in the direction of providing a satisfactory measure of reform.
Why is it that all through the discussion in all these years no progress has been made in the matter of reforming the Senate? The answer is to be found largely in the fact that there has never been proposed any system which would be acceptable to the country as a whole. It is conceded on all hands that in order to bring about any measure of Senate reform acceptable to the country at large such a proposal would have to meet with the approval of the different provinces. And how are we to arrive at anything of that nature? In discussing this matter, it seems to me that the most logical thing to do if we are to make any headway at all would be to consult the people. What are the chief functions of the second chamber? It has been already stated that one of those functions is to revise hasty legislation. But can we find on an examination of our parliamentary history any instance in which the Senate as it is now constituted has discharged that function? I think we shall all agree that so far as revising hasty legislation is concerned the Senate has not served any purpose of that kind. Again, I wish to quote a distinguished leader of the Liberal party on this point. Speaking in a similar debate in 1906 Sir Wilfrid Laurier, referring to the Senate as an institution for the revision of hasty legislation, said:
But this is an idea which has never made much impression on my judgment at all events. Considering the course of such legislatures in the Dominion which are composed of a single branch, elected by the people -the legislatures of Ontario, Manitoba, British Columbia, and some others-I do not believe that we need seriously apprehend any danger from the existence of one branch only of the legislature.
We have, I think, all agreed that the Senate as it is at present constituted does not discharge the functions of a body whose purpose is to revise hasty legislation and to act as the champion of provincial rights and minorities; and the fact that some measure of Senate reform is necessary is borne out by the proposal in the Speech from the Throne to call an interprovincial conference in the recess to deal with this and similar matters. This being the case, I do not think there should be any hesitation on the part of this House in adopting a resolution looking to that end. While I approve of the declaration of the government, that it intends calling this inter-

provincial conference, I do think that the better method of proceeding would be to take a vote of the people of the different provinces in the first instance. How would the delegates to this proposed interprovincial conference know what the views of the people in their respective provinces might be regarding the question of Senate reform? I have grave doubts, for instance, whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and, say, the Attorney General of Ontario, if they met in consultation on a matter of this kind, would be in a position to represent the will of the people of Ontario on the question. I have no reason to know what the opinions of these gentlemen may be on this question, but I have strong reasons to suspect that the feeling of Ontario is greatly in favour of the abolition of the Senate, and I do not know that the Prime Minister and the Attorney General of Ontario are of that mind. I say therefore that before any interprovincial conference is called, or before any such conference can properly function, it is indispensable that the government should first learn the will of the people of the various provinces which would be represented at the gathering.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis). Of all the motions before the House, the subamendment is yet the best solution, and for want of a better one, I sincerely -give it my approval.
However, I think it behooves this Parliament, when it is a question of possible amendments to our constitution in regard to the Senate, to invite the provinces to a conference in order to inquire as to the need of these amendments. I do not approve of this subamendment for the same reasons given ;by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis), but I do so on entirely different grounds. It is well, if for no other reason than courtesy towards the contracting parties of the British North America Act, that the provinces be consulted when it is a question of important amendments as the one which refers to Senate reforms, and, on these grounds I think, we should submit this question to the provinces. Moreover, if such a conference had no other result but amendments in regard to the representation of the provinces it would equally, be proper to consult the provinces.
It is a fact, Sir that a certain agitation has taken place in regard to the upper house, and it is perhaps well at this time that parliament should consult the provinces so as to settle once for all that our constitution, as it exists to-day, is still the best and that we have no reason to amend it. It would perhaps be the best means of putting an end to this agitation.
The Senate

On March 23, 1923, the hon. member for Joliette moved in this House a resolution asking for the reform of the Senate. He wished to have the Senate elective, so that senators should be elected for six years in special electoral divisions, half of them being returned every three years. I must say that the hon. member adopts, to-day, an attitude which is in keeping with the stand he took in i923. He is most sincere in his convictions and I congratulate him in rising again to-day in the House to support a motion for a reform based on the same grounds as in 1923.
I had the honour, at that time, to move the adjournment of the debate. If I had spoken then, I would have done so in the same way as to-day, I would have said that this reform must be proceeded with the greatest precaution and only after a conference with the provinces. I am attached to our constitution, I like the British North America Act such as it is, because it is a pact agreed upon by the provinces, a solemn pact under which our legislative powers are defined and which confides certain powers to the provinces and certain others to the Dominion government. This legislative power of the Dominion government is exercised by the King, the Senate and the House of Commons. The Fathers of Confederation had an aim in view, in 1867, when they created a Senate composed of members appointed for life and chosen by the Governor in Council, and the reasons given at the time were very sound. After many a long discussion, at that time, between the representatives of the various provinces, it was agreed to compromise by creating an upper house composed of life members appointed by the Governor in Council. Had we thought of following the example of other countries, we could have turned our eyes beyond the 45th parallel and seen a Senate with an organization different from that of our upper house; we might have found in other countries an elective Senate; but I think, the Fathers of Confederation were right in giving us an independent upper house, composed of senators appointed for life. I prefer our constitution to that of other countries. The constitution of 1867 is much better than the * one in force in the neighbouring republic or that of other nations. I am attached to our constitution and the manner in which the Senate is constituted, because I think we have in this organization an upper house composed of men unswayed by influences. Such is the opinion of all those who have made a study of the constitution of 1867. The distinctive character of the upper house is that its members are independent; they are legislators as independent as one can find in a country.
TMr. Fortier.]
They are independent because they are appointed for life and chosen by the Governor in Council, and, they have over and above the representatives of the lower house, this liberty of conscience necessary to a legislator which gives him the freedom on certain occasions to resist popular passion and to stick to the veiy last to his convictions for the welfare of his country. I have been told-not that I have personal knowledge of the fact because when I compare my way of thinking with that of my electors I must say that there is nothing that divides us-I have been told that it may happen that a member might be forced to take, under certain circumstances, an attitude contrary to his personal convictions. Yes, this may happen. We represent, in the House of Commons, a section of the country, various elements which, at times, may demand from members a certain line of conduct on a public question. The freedom of action of the members of the lower house is thereby curtailed. It is well to have some display of independence and to state that a member occupies a seat in the House so as to express his personal views, but when the said member returns to his county to ask for a renewal of his mandate, will not the elector call him to task for having aired his personal views contrary to the wish of a faction or party of an electoral district? I would not have thought of it myself if my attention had not been drawn to such a fact, for in aill my political career never did such a case present itself where my electors bad not in me this entire confidence with which they always entrusted me. Here, as well as in Quebec, I had but to rise to express my views in regard to legislation introduced and I always found myself heart and soul in accord with the wishes of the electors of my county. I cannot imagine that at any time, I might have to set aside my personal convictions, for when I express them, I express those of my electors; I trust in them as they trust in me. It is nevertheless a fact that a representative of the people may at times be called upon to handle with tact public passion roused by certain issues and he is thus unable to entirely assert his views. On the other hand, the representative in the upper house, the senator appointed for life, is totally independent. On all issues brought before the Senate, he can enjoy full liberty of conscience and freedom of action. I think it is a well established fact that the existence of an upper house is sometimes very necessary. At times, the Commons obliged to surrender to popular clamour, adopts certain legislation, however it does so with the conviction that the Senate will deal with such a measure on its merits, that it will,

The Senate
if necessary, throw it out if it considers in its wisdom and from its unbiased viewpoint that such a measure is contrary to the interest of the country.
This is one reason why I am the more pledged to upholding the British North America Act and to maintaining the Senate as constituted.
Since reference has been made to constitutional law, I shall take the liberty of quoting a few comments which sum up the views of all those who have made a special study of our Constitution:
The part played by the Senate, as a legislative body, is about the same as that of the House of Lords in England. It has the well defined right to throw out any measure passed by the House of Commons, however, it exercises its powers with prudence and discretion. We are indebted to it for the rejection of quite a number of bills inspired by ill-considered zeal or the effervescence of public opinion. With us, the ponderation of powers is settled; the Senate, in regard to legislation is absolutely the equal of the House of Commons and it has the advantage over the latter of being mdependent of both the power and passions of the people. If it takes its part seriously it may render us important services.
Let us now, Mr. Speaker, consider how the upper house is, at present, constituted. Does the fact of its members being appointed by the Governor in Council lower it in the esteem of the citizens of this country? Does it not compare favourably with any other chamber both in dignity and usefulness? What higher authority than the Governor in Council can make the appointment of senators. It has been stated in this debate that the upper house might be better constituted if the provincial governments were entrusted with the selection of its members or if the government requested people of high standing in this country to join them as advisers for the purpose of appointing senators. Let us be rid forever of these so called all important people without responsibilities whatsoever to advise on the appointment of members to the Senate! The best guarantee we have that the upper house is composed of citizens able to fulfil their important duties, is that the appointment of senators is left to the government. Moreover it is the government, holding ministerial responsibility, who appoint the -members to the Senate, and the government represent authority, established power, in fact the country. Indeed, we have no fault to find as to appointments made up to now, for most of the time-and the government has been well guided in the matter-senators have been chosen amongst members of t'he House of Commons; it is precisely here where they are recruited in greater number.

It is without doubt the best system. Rightly has the government, in numerous instances, appointed to the Senate members who enjoyed the full confidence of their electors and had faithfully served their country during a great number of years.
It is apparent that members of this House, who have been here for a long time and have built up an enviable reputation, are most qualified to sit in the upper house, and we may rest assured that they will allow only sound legislation to be enacted. The course followed by all governments-this one as well as others that have preceded it-is the best; it is a pledge that the Senate will always be composed of worthy and experienced men, the custom followed being to select among the well deserving servants of the state, either in the House or anywhere else. I, therefore, trust, Mr. Speaker, that we shall maintain the present system of appointments to the upper house which exists since Confederation and to which there is no reason- I again state-to effect any changes.
When the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) spoke, a short while ago, with so much enthusiasm upon his subamendment, he stated, as he had done with such eloquence in 1923, that he thought the whole of the province of Quebec was behind him on this question of Senate reform. I shall not wound him by asking him to lay a wager-because I know he is very strongly adverse to wagers- but I shall take upon myself to inform him that he is greatly in error, because the province of Quebec is, by tradition, in favour of maintaining the constitution and the Senate as they are. For all the above reasons I shall vote for the sufoamendiment.
