I should like to join with hon. members in congratulating the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) on the way he presented this matter this afternoon. I must say that I find myself in almost perfect accord with the views he expressed both as to the desirability of the second chamber and as to the method of reform which he, perhaps I should not say advocated, but suggested. I think it was wisdom on his part to introduce the resolution in this negative form. By introducing it in that way, he wished to give us an opportunity to express ourselves as to the present condition of things without any reference at all to possible changes that might be made. I know it has been urged by some who have already spoken that the resolution of the



The Senate
hon. member for West Calgary did not go far enough because it did not advocate any definite proposal. They claim that there is practical unanimity in regard to the resolution as placed upon the order paper. That may be so. I hope it is so, but it seems to me it would have been well worth while, if that be the case, that we should have had a clear-cut plain statement going forth to the country that the Commons of Canada are not satisfied with things as they are at present. Instead of being able to express ourselves on that clear, plain, simple proposition, we have had the matter somewhat entangled by amendments and subamendments. I think our experience of a week ago has shown us that we sometimes get into almost inextricable confusion with amendments and subamendments, and it might possibly be that some members will find themselves again in an embarrassing position. I greatly regret, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members have seen fit at this stage to introduce any amendment, because it does not leave us free to express ourselves on the clear-cut proposition that the Senate of Canada as appointed, and as at present constituted, does not meet the needs of the Canadian people. Are we unanimous on that subject? I believe we are. Certainly the government committed themselves to that proposition when, in the Speech from the Throne, they promised that a conference of the provinces on the subject would be called. So far as those who sit in this corner of the House are concerned, we earnestly endorse the principle, and I have some reason to believe that those who sit on my right, the Conservative party, are also behind this proposition. Certainly their leader is on record at one time as having endorsed the proposition for the total abolition of the Senate, and if that statement is questioned-

Perhaps the House would
like to have my authority for that statement. In January, 1909, Mr. E. A. Lancaster of Lincoln and Niagara, introduced a resolution in the House which, after a long preamble, concluded in this way:
We therefore respectively pray that the said British North America Act be so amended as to provide for the abolition of the said Senate.
That proposition was debated at considerable length, and at the close of the debate was voted upon and the proposition was defeated by some 22 to 111. Among the 22 I find the name of Mr. Meighen. If that is not the right hon. gentleman who now leads

the opposition, then of course my most humble apology is due to him. I am the last man in this House who will deny to any man the right to change his mind; but if his mind on this subject has been changed we will naturally expect to hear from him; but until we have a definite announcement as to such a change we will hold that the Conservative party, as represented by their leader, is in favour of the proposition that the Senate as at present constituted is not for the welfare of Canada. I should like to suggest that we have some reason to believe that the Senate itself would be behind such a proposition. The hon. member for West Calgary this afternoon mentioned the fact that Hon. Sir Richard Scott is on record as having recognized the necessity for Senate reform. I might quote the following in this connection. Hon. Sir Richard Scott moved in the Senate a resolution beginning:
That, in the opinion of the Senate the time has arrived for so amending the constitution of this branch of parliament as to bring the mode of selection of senators more into harmony with public opinion.
Not only was Sir Richard Scott in favour of Senate reform, but we have also Sir Richard Cartwright on record as at one time being in favour of it; and I have no evidence that he changed his mind, although he occupied a place in the Senate. Mr. Lancaster, speaking on the resolution which he introduced to the House, referred to the fact that Sir Richard Cartwright, upon the eve of a general election, speaking in Massey Hall, Toronto, used this language:
The Senate was a millstone around the neck of the Canadian people which he prayed that Providence would soon remove.
Mr. Lancaster goes on to say, somewhat humorously:
I presume the right hon. gentleman is still praying. But he is not praying in the form in which this House should pray, by a concrete motion to bring about a result. And if I may say so, without being flippant, I do not think that the locality in which he is praying is quite consistent with his prayer, for he is now a member of the chamber which he hoped Providence would abolish.
I referred to the debate that took place in the House on Mr. Lancaster's motion, when the right hon. leader of the opposition voted in favour of abolition. I find in the same connection. another well known gentleman, Mr. Sharpe of Lisgar. Mr. Sharpe also voted in favour of the abolition of the Senate, and he too occupies a seat in that honourable body. Now, until we have evidence that these men have changed their minds we can only believe that they accepted these positions in the conviction that they could serve the country there better than anybody else.

The Senate
We must take it therefore that these and other hon. gentlemen, when the time comes, will willingly throw up the life appointment which they evidently accepted1 in the public interest. We must believe that when there is a sufficiently strong public demand they will resign their seats and do what they can to bring about the reforms which we advocate.
The hon. member for West Calgary very wisely pointed out the anomaly that exists in the Senate as it is at present constituted, its chief function supposedly being that of protecting provincial rights. Surely it is anomalous that a body should be specially charged with the protection of provincial rights when it is in no way responsible to the provinces. During a debate that was held in the session following that in which Mr. Lancaster's motion was debated, Sir Wilfrid Laurier made some remarks in this connection. There was introduced into the House by Mr. M. Y. McLean of Huron a resolution very similar to the one we have before us at the present time-
That, in the opinion of this House, the Dominion Senate as at present constituted is not in accordance with the representative institutions of this country, and the government should take the necessary proceedings to have the Senate made representatives of and directly responsible to the people.
In this connection Sir Wilfrid Laurier, while defending the system of appointments, made these remarks:
I will go further and I will give this as my very deliberate opinion, that if there is to be a reform of the Senate it should be in line with the purpose for which the Senate was instituted in this country, that is to say, to protect minorities, and to make it representative of the provinces rather than any other body of men.
He closed the debate with these words:
I am prepared to approach this question without any bias, and I am prepared to have the question examined whether or not, while we should keep the nominative appointment in the government, we should give a share of the responsibility to the different provinces. That is a suggestion which is well worthy of consideration. I agree with my hon. friend that something should be done. This is the last of the reforms which we promised the country, and which we have not yet carried out. It is a reform which we are anxious to carry out, but we wish to carry it out on lines which, I think, would be more in consonance with the spirit of our constitution.
That mtoti'on was not voted upon but was withdrawn. The member for West Calgary, in offering suggestions for possible reform, alluded' to the constitution of the Irish Senate. When the act constituting that body went through the British parliament the constitution of the Irish Senate was brought to my notice and it made a more favourable impression upon my mind than any proposition 59i	,	,
I bad1 seen presented up to that time. I think there is much in it that is well worth our consideration, and in my judgment that plan that has worked in the case of the Irish Free State, with the modifications that would be necessary to suit our conditions, might very well serve the purpose we have in view.
I think, Mr. Speaker, it would be well worth while for me to read from the British statutes a few clauses of that act relating to the constitution of the Irish Senate. The British statutes in this form are not very rleadily available to many sections of our people, .but Hansard is now widely circulated through the country, amd if this matter is to be understood by the people it is well that they should have access to the British statute constituting the Senate of the Irish Free State. For that reason I shall ask leave to place it on Hansard, and in the meantime I propose to read a few clauses of the act.
Article 82
(a)	The first Seaimd Eireann shall consist of sixty members, of whom thirty shall be elected and thirty shall be nominated.
(b)	The thirty nominated members of Seanad Eireann shall be nominated by the president of the Executive Council who shall, in making such nominations, have special regard to the providing of representation for groups or parties not then adequately represented in Dail Eireann.
(c)	The thirty elected members of Seanad Eireann shall be elected by Dail Eireann voting on principles of proportional representation.
(d)	Of the thirty nominated members, fifteen to be selected by lot, shall hold office for the full period of twelve years, the remaining fifteen shall hold office for the period of six years.
(e)	Of the thirty elected members the first fifteen
elected shall hold office for the period of nine years, the remaining fifteen shall hold office for the period of three years.	[DOT]
(f)	At the termination of the period of office of any such members, members shall be elected in their place in manner provided by article 32 of this constitution.
(g)	Casual vacancies shall be filled in manner provided by article 34 of this constitution.
There are four short articles referring to this matter. It will be noticed that the article I have read has reference only to the first Irish Senate. After it is constituted these rules will apply:
Article 30
The Irish Senate shall be composed of citizens who shall be proposed on the grounds that they have done honour to the nation by reason of useful public services or that, because of special qualifications or attainments, they represent important aspects of the nation's life^
Article 31
The number of members of the Irish Senate shall be sixty. A citizen to be eligible for membership of the Irish Senate must be a person eligible to become a member of Dail Eireann, and must have reached the age of thirty-five years. Subject to any provision for the constitution of the first Irish Senate the term of office of a member of the Irish Senate shall be twelve years.
The Senate

Article 32
One-fourth of the members of Seanad the Irish Senate shall be elected every three years from a panel constituted as hereinafter mentioned at an election at which the area of the jurisdiction of the Irish Free State shall form one electoral area, and the elections shall be held on principles of proportional representation.
I shall refer to that again. Article 33 provides for the panel:
Before each election of members of the Irish Senate a panel shall be formed consisting of (a) Three times as many qualified persons as there are members to be elected, of whom two-thirds shall be nominated by Dail Eireann voting according to principles of proportional representation and one-third shall be nominated by the Irish Senate voting according to principles of proportional representation; and
(b) Such persons who have at any time been members of the Irish Senate (including members about to retire) as signify by notice in writing addressed to the president of the Executive Council their desire to be included in the panel.
I am satisfied that some modification of this scheme could be well applied to our own situation. Granting that we accept the provision that the representation should be made more directly by the provinces, why should we not have a province, such as Manitoba, with a given number of senators, constituted into one electoral division, just as is done in the case of the Free State. Nominations would be made under a system agreed upon and then the requisite number of senators elected according to proportional representation. I know proportional representation is anathema to some bon. gentlemen who sit in this House.

I am quite satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that proportional representation in such a case would secure the desired result of having the members of the Senate from any given province representative of the thought, feeling and desires of its people. I am not satisfied that it wouild be well for us to depart from the principle of representation by population. That has been suggested, and the United States has been cited as an example. It is true that if the functions of the Senate were only to protect state rights, then the fact of the smaller states having equal representation with the larger might ensure their interests not being jeopardized by the action of the larger states. But the Senate of the United States does not by any means confine its activities to protecting the rights of the smaller states. And when it comes to dealing with larger matters of policy, I

cannot at present see that it would be wise for us to depart altogether from the principle of representation by population. It may be that the numbers are too large as at present, although even that may be a matter of doubt.
I hope Mr. Speaker, that if we can vote on the original proposition as submitted to the House we will have an absolutely unanimous expression of opinion, and while that may not satisfy some hon. members, it seems to me it would be no small achievement, for it would go forth to the country that on this matter the Commons of Canada are not in favour of things as they are.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other members, I should like to congratulate my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) on bringing this important matter before the House. I am not so sure that I can congratulate him on his tolerance of the Senate. With the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), I should like to see everyone have an opportunity of stating his position either in regard to Senate reform or possibly to its abolition.
What is all the hue and cry about? Why is it that since 1874 various resolutions have been brought forward in this chamber and long discussions have taken place with respect to Senate reform, and yet in the end nothing has been done? What has brought this important subject once more before the public, what has focused their attention upon that honourable body? It is because in the past that honourable body has nullified certain legislation passed by this chamber. It seems to me that no matter how you may endeavour to reform the Senate, just so long as you have such a body enjoying that prerogative the wishes of the people will be thwarted. I have before me at the present time a statement of the number of bills thrown out by the Senate since 1867-about fifty-seven years-numbering approximately 150. Some of those measures, of course, were of minor importance, but many of them were of major importance and would have been of decided advantage to the Canadian people had they been placed on the statute book of this fair Dominion. It cannot be expected that the Senate will acquiesce in everything that this House does, otherwise it would be simply a duplication of the legislative machinery; and if we are to have a second chamber without power either to initiate or nullify legislation, the only logical course, it seems to me, is to abolish that second chamber.
Of course, arguments have been advanced against the abolition of the Senate, and those in favour of its retention tell us that a second

The Senate
chamber is necessary to check hasty legislation. But I cannot see any reason for an intelligent democracy such as ours to have its representatives held in check by an appointive body. If that body was removed altogether this chamber would be far more careful in passing legislation. There are many instances on record where parliament has passed legislation with the direct intention that it shall be nullified by the Senate, the object being to make political capital. It seems to me that the only ground upon which the issue can be sidestepped is that of political expediency; it cannot be done if the wishes of the people or the well-being of the country are kept in mind.
That the Senate exists to safeguard the interests of the provinces was a point brought out, I believe, by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) as well as by the hon. member for West Calgary. Well, when the Senate had an opportunity to safeguard the interests of the three great prairie provinces, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, in connection with their natural resources, they failed miserably. That was the time when they should have stood four-square to the wind and have seen to it that these three provinces entered the confederation on the same basis as the other provinces. If those responsible for this resolution rest their case on the argument that the Senate exerts its prerogative against the wishes of the people, the only logical thing to do is not to reform the Senate but to abolish it.
In his trip west, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) once again stirred up public opinion and focused attention on the Senate by his references to the subject, and a great many people out there hoped that something definite would be done by this parliament. Of course, the more serious minded people realized that this parliament could not accomplish anything of itself; that the only constitutional way to reform or to 'abolish the Senate was to call a conference of the provinces. Apparently the Prime Minister has also reached that conclusion, because what he hoped to do was announced in the Speech from the Throne this year. It seems to me that this is the only logical way out. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) in a speech delivered last year, pointed out that under the British North America Act the Parliament of Canada consists of both Houses and the only way to reform or abolish the one or the other is to get the consent of the parties to the confederation, namely, the provinces. He showed that the power was not given this parliament to change the constitution of either House.
Senate Teform involves a constitutional question. This aspect of the matter was discussed the other day and I shall not enter very fully into it. There was no unanimity in the discussion that took place in the House on that occasion. Constitutional lawyers and other lawyers and hon. members generally expressed their views, but no definite conclusion was arrived at. Since abolition of the Senate is really out of the question, logical as it may seem to be, I wish to refer for a few moments to certain reforms that I think might be considered.
The hon. member for West Oalgary read a part of the speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) dealing with this question. You will remember that the Minister of Finance, speaking two years ago, said that the Senate was a check, not a block; that our country was variously constituted, the people of different sections of the country having different ideas on many questions, and that it was necessary to have a senate in order to place a check upon hasty legislation. Well, have they really checked any hasty legislation? In 1919 legislation which had the effect of taking away the right of trial by jury of persons born outside of Canada was passed in this House, and it was also passed in the other chamber in almost less than an hour. They failed miserably to check that legislation. Some years afterwards when we of the Progressive party came into this House we attempted to repeal that legislation, which we regarded as a blot upon the fair name of British and Canadian people, but that attempt was blocked; so I submit that the Senate has miserably failed either to check hasty legislation or-in many cases- to permit the passing of legislation of real value to the Canadian people.
The government has promised to proceed along constitutional lines, and I do not see the value of continuing this discussion unless it be to give the government the benefit of the opinion of representatives of the people when the conference of the provinces is held during the summer. I can readily understand that if this body is to continue to exist it must have certain power and it must have the right to safeguard the provinces. Some measure of control must rest with the second chamber. But when a measure has been before the people and has been discussed by them; when an issue has been placed before the electors and they have decided upon it in no uncertain way by returning representatives who, they believe, will introduce those views in the form of legislation, then I do not think it is logical that there should be any power on the part of another body to
The Senate

nullify that legislation. Of course if a government introduces legislation that has not been fully considered by the people, then the second chamber, if we are to have one, should have the right to nullify that legislation until such time as the electors have an opportunity to examine it fully. Subsequently, if there is no hue and cry against it; if no serious objection is urged, in the following session this House should have the right to introduce that legislation again and enact it into law.
The hon. member for West Calgary was on good ground when he referred to the equalization of representation among the provinces. I do not see any reason why Ontario and Quebec should dominate all the rest of Canada. I believe myself that the only fair thing to do would be to give equal representation to each of the provinces, especially since it is claimed that the Senate exists for the safeguarding of the provinces. I do not agree, if we are going to have a second chamber, that a membership of thirty-six would be sufficient. Canada is a great country and it would be very difficult for four representatives from each province to keep in touch with affairs in all the provinces. If there is to be a second chamber I believe those who represent the provinces should be able to keep fully in touch with them; accordingly eight or ten representatives at least for each province would be necessary to safeguard the interests of the people.
With regard to the election of the Senate, I do not see that that is at all practicable or desirable. The people have already spoken as to who should represent them in parliament; they have elected their representatives to the House of Commons. Shall they elect another body to supervise or exercise jurisdiction over the first? It does not seem to me to be necessary or even logical to have two bodies of men, both representatives of the people and one working against the other. An elective Senate would be a duplication of this chamber. I have before me the complexion of the Senate, not the political complexion, but the interests they represent. If we are going to have a Senate, it should be representative of the masses, and I would like to ask, how many representatives have the farmers of this country got in the Senate? The agriculturists number at least 52 per cent of the whole of Canada, but how many representatives of agriculture can you find in that chamber? How many working men can be found in the Senate to-day? Surely they have a right to be represented there; surely the farmers have a right to be represented there. If you will go over the list, you will find that the great majority of the men comprising the

Senate are lawyers. I have nothing to say against the lawyers; they have a right to be represented there just as much as anybody else, if we are going to have a chamber of that kind; but if we are going to have representatives of the people in that chamber we have a right to see that our representatives are there. I have before me a tabulation based upon the Parliamentary Guide and the Annual Canadian Financial Review, showing the directorships which members of the Senate hold. This tabulation shows that Senators hold 266 directorships in various companies. This may seem to show that they are representative business men, but I contend that it shows also that the interests of these companies and of the great industries of this country are very particularly represented in the second chamber, and if you want any proof of that, without mentioning any names I can pick at random the directorships that some of these men hold. Take Mr. A., for instance who according to the Parliamentary Guide is a Conservative. He is a director in the following companies: Fire Insurance Company of Canada; North Railway Company; Dominion Steel Corporation; Atlantic Sugar Refinery; Canada Car & Foundry Company, Limited; Ames Holden, Limited; The Insurance Company of Canada; Mount Royal Hotel Company; Capital Trust Company; Dominion Coal Company; Nova Scotia Steel & Coal Company; Eastern Car Company; Acadia Coal Company, Limited. This one individual, Mr. A, a representative of the people, holds thirteen directorships; so I think these companies are ably represented in the Senate. I say that it would be most difficult so long as we have that type of man in the Senate to pass bills affecting any of these interests.
Here is another member of the Senate, Mr. B, a Liberal. He is a director in the following companies:	Canada Cement Company; British Empire Steel Corporation; Reliance Insurance Company of Canada; Canada Steamships Company. Here is another, Mr. C, a Conservative, who is a director in the following companies: Rhodes Curry, Company; Canada Car & Foundry Company; Canadian Steel Foundries, Limited; The Pratt & Lackworth Company, Limited; Canadian Land Company; Bank of Nova Scotia; Canadian Light & Power Company; Canadian Accident & Fire Insurance Company; Cuban Canadian Sugar Company; Montreal Trust Company; Montreal Tramways & Power Company; Travellers Life Association of Canada. What I want to make known to the Canadian people is this, that these men who have been appointed to the Senate by both Liberal and Conservative governments are

Mr. Speaker, the question at present uhder consideration is most worthy of our attention. For a number of years past the question of Senate reform has been discussed, however, up to now nothing has been done to reform this institution which dates back to 1867, year of the Confederation.
The present government has understood and is fully aware that nothing can be done without first consulting the provinces which are contracting parties to the British North America Act. Therefore, nothing can be accomplished without their consent. This is why the Speech from the Throne mentions that the House will in the course of this session be called upon to sanction the meeting of a conference between the Dominion * and provincial governments in order to consider the opportunity of amending the constitution of the Senate. Without considering the chances of success of such a conference, I 'think, Mr. Speaker, it is the only consistent course for us to follow. I shall not enter into the arguments for and against the project of the reform of the Senate which have been presented to this House, but I shall take the liberty of briefly expressing my personal views which are shared by a very large majority of my electors as well as those of my province. These views are that we should not interfere with the confederation pact and, in particular, the constitution of the Senate that we hold as the guardian of our rights.
I shall, therefore, for the above reasons vote for the subamendment, against the amendment and resolution.
The intention of the government is so clearly expressed in the Speech from the Throne that it seems to me that it should have been understood and the resolution should not 'have given rise to such a debate in the House. True, such a subject affords a splendid opportunity to some of our able debaters, but has very little economic interest for the country at large.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: In the Senate as at present constituted there are 24 members representing Ontario, 24 representing Quebec, 10 representing New Brunswick, 10 representing Nova Scotia, 4 representing Prince Edward Island, and 6 each for the four western provinces, or 96 in all. Nine millions of Canadians have the same number of senators as one hundred and ten millions of Americans. The members of our Senate are selected by the government of Canada really as a reward for partisan services; they are not elected at all by the provinces they purport to represent. And furthermore-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will
keep his seat and pay attention I think I will answer every question he may put. I repeat, all our senators are selected, by the government of Canada as a reward for partisan services, and not at all by the provinces they purport to represent. Furthermore appointees must be acceptable to members of the government representing Ontario and Quebec which provinces to-day hold half the veto power of the whole Dominion. The senators are all appointed for life. True they may resign but this is not very likely. The purpose of the Senate was primarily to protect the weaker provinces by preventing hasty legislation, and to temper the national action with national caution. That it has failed in this purpose is seen in the fact that it has tempered national action with partisan caution. That the Senate has failed to protect the weaker provinces is seen in the fact that it is controlled by the two major provinces of the Dominion, Ontario and Quebec, by the method of appointment, and also by the excessive representation of these two provinces. The excessive representation of Ontario and Quebec has, up to this time, served no legitimate purpose and is useless for any other purpose than domination. The Senate has maintained its domination of Canada by Ontario and Quebec, in conjunction with the domination by these two provinces in the House of Commons since confederation. This domination has made these two old provinces-or the old union of Ontario and Quebec-think consciously and sub-consciously of Canada in terms of two provinces only. It has really prevented these provinces from realizing the viewpoint of the other provinces. It has made them incapable of taking an ocean to ocean viewpoint of this Dominion, it has

The Senate
imbued them with an unwillingness to conciliate and compromise, and they are ever ready to use their power to dominate. These evidences of political unfitness are specially characteristic of the citizens of Montreal and Toronto, and the effect this has had upon the policies of Canada is that it has made them sectional rather than national. It has evolved a national policy based on the establishment of an industrial area within Ontario and Quebec, unique among industrial areas in that it is not founded on iron, or steel, or coal, it has imposed tariff restrictions and custom regulations on the whole of Canada for its own benefit, almostly exclusively for the advantage of this one industrial area. It has imposed or prompted the imposition of transportation rates both by rail and water, rates well calculated to prevent the establishment of industrial areas in other parts of the Dominion where coal and iron are abundant. It has evolved a domestic policy based on the appropriation of the public domain of the unborn provinces, and which has resulted in the disposition of very large areas of this public domain as public lands for Dominion purposes on the false assumption that these western areas were purchased and annexed by the Dominion instead of being admitted into the union of Canadian provinces. I refer to Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territory. In pursuance of that domestic policy the balance of confederation has been disturbed by increasing the area of the two major provinces out of all proportion, and has delivered to them for their sole use and benefit the public domain within the areas included by the extension of their boundaries.
It twice goaded the native inhabitants of Rupert's Land into rebellion as a protest against domination; and by persistent disallowance of provincial railway charters and prevention of railway competition all but precipitated an armed conflict at Fort Whyte in Manitoba in the early eighties. From the Atlantic to the Pacific disunion has resulted from the domestic policy of subordinating all other interests to those of the dominating provinces, a policy which has so recently found aggravating expression in preventing extension of branch lines of the Canadian National railway to productive areas lacking transportation; and in preventing competitive transportation routes by way of the Panama canal and Hudson bay.
What is the remedy? Real Senate reform: the replacement of the present Senate by one in which every province, large or small, will be represented on the floor of the Senate
by the same number of senators, preferably not more than five or six for each province. This is no new idea. It has been the basis of representation in the Senate of the United States since 1789. It is the basis of Senate representation in Australia and South Africa except as to representation of the natives in South Africa. It is the system adopted by all or nearly all nations having federal government except our own, and it is enunciated and but partially applied in our constitution. Sir Wilfred Laurier suggested this reform in the parliamentary sessions of 1906, 1908 and 1909. On both occasions he was discussing as premier, certain resolutions before the House of Commons relating to Senate abolition and Senate reform. In 1906 this great statesman said, among other things:
A second chamber seems to me absolutely necessary for two reasons. It is supposed to be a check on hasty legislation, but one consideration [DOT]which to my mind is absolutely conclusive and paramount is that under our system, composed of federal units, a second chamber is an absolutely necessary safeguard against a possible invasion of the rights of the smaller provinces. But if we are to have reform, I would not be averse to adopting the system of our neighbours and have each province represented by an equal number of members, whether that province be large or small.
In the session 'of 1907-08 Sir Wilfrid Laurier is reported by Hansard, page 1570, as having
said:
In the United States Senate, the state of New York has two members, and the state of Rhode Island has also two members, so that while in the House of Representatives each state speaks according to the numerical strength of its population-
Thirty-six against two.
-in the Senate each state has an equal voice.
He further states:
If I had to offer a reform it would be that all the provinces should be represented by an equal number of senators. There are nine provinces, and if each province were represented by, let us say six senators, that would give us a senate of fifty-four members, which would be a pretty strong body, a body sufficiently large and not cumbersome.
He further said:
I would like to ask the House to consider this proposition: that the number of senators ought to be limited to a fixed number, and that each province should be represented in the Senate by an equal number of senators. I mentioned six, but that is arbitrary; it may be five or it may be seven, or it may be eight, or it may be ten; I do not care which for the present moment. But what I would insist on is that each province should be represented by an equal number of senators.
He said further:
Beyond this and the suggestion that the appointment should not be for life but for a limited period I would not be prepared to go.
That Sir Wilfrid did not go the length we thought he was prepared to go in Senate re-



The Senate
form is due to the fact that it would have involved a change conferring on the provinces that right to equal Senate representation for which they had not asked, but for which they have a perfect right to ask. Canada is a federal union of nine provinces, legalized by the British North America Act of 1867. The object of the act was neither to weld the provinces into one nor to subordinate provincial governments to a centrail authority. It was to create a federal government in which all should be represented, such government to be entrusted with the exclusive administration of affairs within its own jurisdiction. The provinces were to have a common interest, each retaining its independence and autonomy, and these independent autonomous provinces have a right to seek changes in the constitution of that branch of the Parliament of Canada composed exclusively of persons appointed to represent them. Amendments have been made to the British North America Act on the address of the Dominion parliament without the -formally expressed consent of the provinces or even of a majority of them. One of these amendments violated a fundamental provision of the federation compact, upon which the British North America Act is based, namely that providing for representation by population in the House of Commons. During the war the Conservative government did secure such an amendment without the formally expressed consent of the provinces. This establishes a precedent that amendments may be made without the formally expressed consent of any of the provinces. It also establishes a precedent that fundamental provisions of the confederation compact may be violated on motion of a parliament of -Canada willing to be guilty of a breach of faith; provided the governments of the provinces again wilfully or negligently -fail to protest. But that does not preclude their formally expressing consent or protest. In respect of any constitutional amendment not involving a change in any of the fundamental provisions of the confederation compact, an, address from, a majority of the provinces asking for such change would weigh; but if a fundamental provision of that compact were involved, addresses from all the provinces would be necessary, or at least the protest of any province should be sufficient to prevent the amendment. By a fundamental provision of the confederation compact I mean that the union of the provinces was voluntary. Those provinces who did not express a desire to be federally united into one dominion were not included until they expressed that desire, Newfoundland is not yet included. Funda-

mental provisions are those, the inclusion of which in the compact was necessary to evoke a desire in any one or more provinces to be federally united with the others. That there should be a Senate was a fundamental provision of the confederation compact. Unanimous consent is necessary to its abolition.
The preponderant representation of Ontario and Quebec in the House of Commons would perpetuate their domination of Canada and make real national union forever impossible. The procedure necessary to reform the Senate requires addresses to the Imperial parliament from the House of Commons and from a majority of the provincial legislative assemblies, all of which being elective have an inherent right to speak for the people and provinces they represent. No address to the Senate is necessary. They being non-elective the Senate has no inherent right to speak for either the provinces as provinces nor for the citizens of Canada as citizens of Canada. It has a right to address the Imperial parliament independently of the House of Commons even as the British House of Commons and the House of Lords have from time to time addressed' His Majesty quite independently of each -other. After all the Senate is a -part of the Parliament of Canada. As such it has had delegated to -it by the British North America Act power to do certain legislative acts, but delegated powers must be construed strictly and addressing the Imperial parliament either in prayer or protest is not a legislative act. Anyone may do it. Amendments to the British North America Act are not amendments to an act of the Parliament of Canada where the consent of the Senate is necessary.
The constitution of Canada is the legal expression of the will of its people as to their machinery of government and its operation, and to allege that the consent of an irresponsible body in no sense representative is necessary to their deposition is to allege that constitutional change cannot be made constitutionally should the people of Canada so will. The fact that they have been appointed for life does not alter the right of the people to change their tenure of office. The tenure of office of other servants of Canada has been shortened, ostensibly in the public interest with the tacit approval of the Senate, and a precedent well established. Consent of the Senate is not necessary. The Imperial parliament will follow its time-honoured policy of bestowing on the dominions, whose equal status it acknowledges, all the powers they ask for. Failure to recognize the expressed will of the people of Canada -as to its machinery of government, or an attempt to

The Senate
make legalization conditional on the continuance of the present Senate in office, would raise a much larger issue than that of Senate reform. When Canada sees fit to cease expending any portion of its revenue in payment of sessional indemnities to appointed senators no British parliament will intervene. Constitutional fictions to the contrary notwithstanding, the fact is that the Briton abroad is not in Canada a subject of the Briton at home. The senators vigorously contend that the Senate cannot be reformed without their consent, but in doing so they are alleging that the Senate cannot be reformed except by revolution.
The reformed Senate should be chosen by proportional representation for fixed terms, not subject to dissolution, with the whole province as the constituency. They should be elected for some fixed period, not less than seven and not more than ten years. Why proportional representation? Proportional representation ensures the representation of minorities, and a Senate so elected will be more considerate of the rights of minorities than one elected by majority vote in single constituencies. It is desirable that it should be, and proportional representation will ensure it. Should each province elect six senators any minority numbering one-sixth of the population would be sure of representation. If partisanship be discriminated against by making senators ineligible for cabinet positions, election by proportional representation should fill the Senate with well assorted senators specially qualified to temper national action with national caution and to conciliate the conflicting interests of the provinces. The very existence of a real federal Senate would itself obviate the need for much conciliation and compromise.
Unlike the House of Commons the votes and proceedings of a real federal Senate will not be an accurate measure of its functioning. Sponsors of bills will inevitably consider before introducing them, their chances to pas the Senate on their merits.
Other unnamed "important particulars" are to be submitted to the conference. The omission from the British North America Act, of categorical mention of those provisions of the act which were fundamental to the confederation compact, should be supplied as one of the next amendments. So soon as, but not before, a Privy Council decision has determined whether the public domain in the three prairie provinces is vested in the crown in the right of the provinces or in the right of the Dominion; so soon as a real federal Senate is established, and provisions have been added to the British North America Act specifying what
provisions of our constitution require unanimous consent for their amendment; and so soon as the act shall have had its deadwood eliminated and its provisions consolidated, provision should be made .for the future amendment of our constitution. This must be made subject to the specified fundamental conditions of the confederation compact, but not before the aforesaid conditions shall have been fulfilled. Those provinces whose minority rights and privileges are incorporated in the British North America Act very naturally require assurance that these rights and privileges shall not be abrogated by a parliamentary majority in Canada. The underprivileged provinces may very properly demand that, before Canada is empowered to amend her own constitution, there shall be no overprivileged and no underprivileged provinces in Canada. The prairie provinces which believe and know that their public domain has been illegally appropriated by the Dominion, naturally do not intend to consent to Canada's being empowered to amend her own constitution until it shall, have become impossible for a Canadian parliamentary majority to confirm Canada's spoliation of the public domain within their respective borders. Unless and until these matters are settled, the conferring on Canada of power to amend her own constitution, will only jeopardize that _ national unity so necessary to the progress and prosperity of Canada. We must do first things first.
What then is the conclusion of the whole matter? That the British North America Act should be amended and consolidated, and that as amended and consolidated it should provide a categorical declaration as to those fundamental provisions of the act which shall not be amendable without the unanimous consent of the provinces. We need real Senate reform, and amendment thereafter by the Parliament of Canada, and for deferring the coming into force of the provision empowering the Dominion parliament to amend the constitution until the respective rights of the Crown, in the right of the provinces, and in the right of the Dominion, to the public domain of the prairie provinces, shall have been determined by the legal tribunal of last resort.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
The question of Senate reform is about as old as confederation. There have been in this country very many people, among them some very eminent statesmen, who during their public and political careers have stood for Senate reform, and the advocates of this reform have been agitating from 1861 up to the present time. But so
The Senate

far there has been, no reform of the Senate, and in my opinion it will be some years yet before there will be any such reform of great importance. And that is due entirely to our constitution as it stands. A great many objections are offered to the present constitution of the Senate. Some of them may be well founded while others are not, but the principal objection as I see it is that the Senate is not in touch with the public pulse, it is not in touch with public opinion, and therefore its decisions on legislation received from the House of Commons is not at all times according to public opinion, Well, Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who think that sometimes even public opinion is astray, and that although a popular outburst may for the time being carry the Commons off its feet, that opinion may not be founded on mature consideration and cool judgment of the question at issue.
I have heard it said to-day by hon. gentlemen, who no doubt have given this question serious consideration, that the Senate should be abolished, indeed, that- it should never have been in existence. Well, I can point to two decisions of the Senate which, I think, have fully justified its creation. May I refer to the gold rush to the Yukon? At that time the public were carried off their feet, they were amazed at the marvellous gold discoveries'in that great northern country, but they did not consider for a moment how long those discoveries were going to continue. Insistent demands were made upon the Liberal government of the day for the building of a railway into the Yukon at a cost of millions of dollars, and public opinion was solidly behind those demands. The great statesman, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was Prime Minister, and a measure for the building of the railway passed this House with very few dissenting votes; but fortunately the Senate killed it. I think by that act alone the Senate fully justified its existence, for undoubtedly by the course they took they demonstrated that they had greater vision than those who at that time thought they were representing public opinion. On that occasion we had a Liberal House of Commons and a Conservative Senate. I do not say that the Senate killed the Yukon railway bill because it came from a Liberal government, for this would be tantamount to saying that any bill originating in this House might be thrown out by the Senate to gain a political advantage. That is not the history of the Senate in its attitude towards legislation initiated in this chamber. Again, in 1913-14 the Senate-then Liberal-threw out a measure introduced by the Conservative government. I happened to 	"*
be a member of this House in those days. I presume, Mr. Speaker, that never in the history of this parliament was there a greater debate than that which became known as the naval debate, when politics was at fever heat. The Conservative government took the position that this country should make a monetary contribution to augment the Imperial navy; the opposition took the stand that we could best help the imperial authorities by organizing a Canadian navy. The bill passed the House of Commons, but the Senate killed it. There again I say the Senate justified its existence.
The speech of my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) was a very fair presentation of the constitutional position respecting the Senate; but I do not agree with him that the Senate is undemocratic. The ideals of democracy, of course, have never been realized in this or any other country; but nowhere in the wide world has democracy achieved a greater practical success than in the British Empire. In this Dominion we have democracy in its truest form, and I am prepared to stand for a constitution which has weathered the storms of political crises and reached its present well-ordered development-the constitution of Great Britain. Some of the greatest statesmen of the world have helped in the development of that constitution which has made England supreme commercially and politically throughout the entire world. If democracy has been a failure, it has been so in those countries which did not have such safeguards as the House of Lords of England and the Senate of Canada. Certain hon. gentlemen referred to some of the European states before the war and to some of those created after the war where they had no second chambers. Well, when it comes to making a choice between the constitution of some of the European countries with unspeakable names and the constitution of Canada, I am for our constitution.
Some speakers on the other side, my Progressive friends I think, urged that the Senate does not feel the public pulse, that it is out of touch with public opinion. Are we so childish in this House, Sir, as to think that by our speeches and our votes we are always truly representing public opinion? For example, next year, the year after,-or ten years hence, a minority in this House may actually be representing the majority of the people. Can it be said that under those circumstances the House of Commons is responsive to public opinion? No. I venture the statement that very often in this House we vote against what we well know to be public opinion in

The Senate
order to satisfy our own conscience-those of us who have any; I hope we all have. After all, public opinion at times is just as mistaken as anything else in this world. I venture to say that on some of the questions that have been debated and voted decided in this House for the past twenty or twenty-five years, very often a private ballot would have resulted in those questions being negatived which were answered in the affirmative. I think that if it had been possible to have had a private ballot on some of the public questions which have been debated and voted on in this House, and which appeared to have public opinion behind them, it would have been a revelation-perhaps not so much to this House as to the country.

speechtext: Oh, responsible government may be a myth. There are different ways of saying what is responsible government. Responsible government has been employed in the past in such a way as to make public opinion. We have responsible government, I say, in this country and in Great Britain on nearly as well developed a basis as we can get it; but like all other earthly institutions, governments-democratic, monarchical, communist or otherwise-make mistakes. If I were to point to the country which made greater progress in a short time than any other I would name the country which for four hundred years was ruled entirely by a senate. Rome became mistress of the world under a senate. She did have the happy faculty, of course, of getting the very best men-statesmen, generals, ambassadors, consular agents; these were the people who made the laws and guided the destinies of Rome. From a mere municipality she grew to be mistress of the world; there was really no civilization outside of Rome. So much for what a senate has done for one country.

Now, one of the cure-alls for the defects of the Senate is alleged to be the appointment of our senators by the provincial legislatures. Well, from what body would they appoint them? What would prevent our legislatures from appointing partisans to the Senate? There is no provincial government that is not more or less partisan, and if a vacancy occurred in the Senate the provincial government would appoint, I have no doubt, a partisan supporter. Would the mere fact that the government or the legislature of a province appointed a senator make him nonpartisan? Would it raise ham above the ordinary man we find in the Senate to-day? I do not see how it could. Under our present system senators are appointed by the Governor in Council, and the appointment must be made from the province where the vacancy occurs. It is part of our constitution that t h e ^ senator must have his residence in the province he represents. By what manipulation of imagination can one conclude that a man would make a better senator from Ontario, from Quebec or from any other province simply because he was appointed by the provincial legislature or the provincial government rather than by the Governor-General-in-Council?
Another reason offered by an hon. member for the abolition of the Senate is that the Senate was designed for the protection of minorities, and he says he has failed in his reading to come across any case in which the interests of the minorities in this country were protected by that body. Well, I have not gone into that question, but I have faith enough in humanity, faith enough in even

the present Senate, faith enough in this country from having read its history, political and otherwise, to come to the conclusion that we have not had and will not have a Senate which would deliberately attempt to dominate minorities in such a way to as take away from them any of their rights.

speechtext: Was it not necessary to change the British North America Act in order to withhold from the newly formed western provinces the right to control their own natural resources?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
If that is so I would
point it out to those who are so very anxious to make it easy to amend the British America Act.
One of the hon. members who spoke on this question urged that there was too large a representation in the Senate, and I think the same hon. member went on to say that all provinces should be equally represented in that body. I do not argue against that principle, but I would point out that there are insur-

mountable difficulties in the way of its adoption. We are told on the best of legal authority that before we can amend the British North America Act we must have the consent of all the provinces. Do youi think that Quebec or Ontario, with their larger populations, would gracefully submit to Prince Edward Island having the same number of representatives in the Senate as they did?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I certainly do not, but just
the same I think Nova Scotia would be in a much better position to-day if she had equal representation in the Senate.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
She might have a preponderance of right on her side. I am not saying anything with respect to Nova Scotia at the moment, but I simply warn my western friends of this:	It may not come in our
generation, but those of us who know anything about the west will have no hesitation in coming to the conclusion that before very many decades the bulk of our population will be west of lake Superior, and then hon. gentlemen from the west who to-day say they have not sufficient representation in the Senate may have another song to sing.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
By that time I hope the
Senate will be abolished.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
My hon. friend has made several assertions. First, he said he wanted the Senate abolished; then he said it could not be abolished in view of a learned opinion given by the hon. member of Hants (Mr. Martell). Then he went on to tell us how the Senate might be reformed in this, that and the other respect. Suppose the hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this debate to-day from the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba,-if any have spoken from Manitoba-suppose they represented the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta and Manitoba; what a nice fix We would be in then! They would undertake to fix the constitution of the Senate, to reform it and do other things. Would there be any unity amongst them? I am simply pointing out the difficulties we will have under our constitution in amending the Senate in any particular.
The mover of this resolution, who has given the subject serious study and is a good sound lawyer, has made a splendid presentation of his case. He did what every man should do when he asks that a change in our constitution be made; he indicated what he thought that change should1 be; but hon. gentlemen who followed him, the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis), the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans), and other hon. gentlemen have not followed him in that

The Senate
respect. It simply goes to show that the way set out in the Speech from the Throne is the only way by which we can arrive at any conclusion as to what amendments the people as a whole or the provinces as a whole are prepared to make. There is very little use in our discussing the question in this House in an academic way. We are going to arrive at no unanimous conclusion because the reforms which we have in our minds are so numerous and so varied that they will not be accepted by one-third of the other members of this House. I believe that eveiy member of this House has some ideal in his mind. Ideals are splendid things to have, but they are difficult to bring into effect. I do not think you could get ten members of this House who would sit down and come to a unanimous conclusion as to what reforms of the Senate they would undertake in order to improve it. That is going to be just our difficulty when we get the representatives of all the provinces together. We talk of public opinion, but whom are we going to get from the provinces to represent public opinion? Does the government of a province represent public opinion in that province? Maybe so, maybe not. Does a provincial government which got its mandate four or five years ago on the question of, say, prohibition-I mention that just for the sake of illustration, I am not sneering at it in any way-would that government represent public opinion in its province to-day on the question of reforming the Senate? This question is far more serious I believe than any person who has not given it serious thought conceives. Let us take the province of Nova Scotia, for example. Supppose there was a conference held at Ottawa to-morrow on the question of Senate reform. The government of Nova Scotia has been in power for five years the next 10th of July. Will anyone say that the government of Nova Scotia could come up here and would fairly represent the people of that province on Senate reform when they say: This is what we think should be done. They might, and they might not, be representing public opinion in that province; I would rather think they would not be representing it, after being four or five years in power without making an appeal to the people of that province.
My own idea is that if we are going to get any Senate reform, we must have a definite and concrete proposal to place before the people of the various provinces, and I think that if we will attempt to live up to our ideals of what a democracy should be, the question should be presented to the people by means 60
of a plebiscite. I would, as a matter of fact, ask the Dominion and provincial governments to set aside a sum of money for the purpose of placing before the people of this country from the constituency of Cape Breton South all the way across the country to Vancouver the pros and cons of the definite and concrete proposal which should be submitted to them. In that way, and in that way only, can you ascertain what public opinion is in this country on the question of Senate reform.
According to the Speech from the Throne,
' perhaps next May or perhaps the middle of June, there will be a conference of provincial premiers, probably accompanied by their provincial secretaries and attorneys general, and possibly by their whole cabinets, held here at Ottawa. They may decide on some concrete proposition. But will any gentleman in this House dare to say that in that they will be representing public opinion in this country?
I say no, decidedly not, for the very good reason that they do not know what public opinion is on this question, and therefore cannot represent it, even though they might stumble into the way of doing what the people think should be done.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
Supposing the question
was submitted in a plebiscite, and one province voted in favour of the retention of the Senate and the others against; what would be the outcome?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: The outcome would be, if my hon. friend is right in the law he gave us in his address the other day, that the Parliament of Great Britain would not grant us a change in our constitution 'by which we could make effective the reform that the majority of the provinces had voted for. That is why I say we are going to be up against a proposition that is far more difficult, far more momentous than we think, perhaps even than the government itself thinks, though I presume they have given this matter serious study.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: If the question were submitted to the people in a plebiscite, and the people of a province should not vote in harmony with the position taken by the government of that province, where would we be then?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Hants asked me the same question in a different way. I say that the Imperial parliament would not consent to the amending of our constitution if any one of the provinces said no to the concrete proposal put before it.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I think the hon.
gentleman hardly caught my question. I said



The Senate
that- supposing within the bounds of one province, in carrying out the plebiscite he suggests, the people should vote in contradiction to the expressed will of the government of that province; which should prevail, the plebiscite or the will of the government?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: If a provincial government consented to the plebiscite and there was a strong majority one way or the other I would say that that government would not dare to enter the conference and say that notwithstanding the popular vote it would take another course.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: How about the temperance act in Ontario?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I have heard that name
before.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
We can compromise on
4.4.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: I am not going to discuss the Ontario Temperance Act m connection with our constitution.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I was referring to the
plebiscite there, and the action of the government, not to the merits of the Ontario Temperance Act.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: That is a proper question but I am not going to say anything about it.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: That has nothing to do with amending the British North America Act.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: If the Premier of Ontario did wrong he will be punished. I am not saying that he did wrong. I think, after reading the speech which he made in the legislature of Ontario the other day, that he is pretty nearly right. However I am not to be led away into a discussion on a question of that kind. I am discussing a concrete proposition as to the reform of the Senate. If we reform the Senate we must amend our constitution, and I am pointing -out some obstacles in the way of that amendment.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman have any Senate reform?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I would not have very
much. I was going to take that point up later. I was dealing with propositions which have emanated from other hon. members, and I was arguing the point that the only way in which we can get the proper pulse of the people of this country on the reform of the Senate, or any other change in our constitution, is by a plebiscite, in view of the fact that we may have governments that should have gone to the country long ago and do not at present represent popular opinion. I am

not mentioning any particular government. I referred to the government of Nova Scotia because it has been the longest in power. I hope it represents public opinion in that province, but it cannot say that it represents public opinion on a question which has never been submitted to the electors of the province, and if we are going to live in accordance with democratic institutions in Canada such a question as this should be submitted to the people.
I was asked the question what amendments I would suggest, and I replied very few. I am not one of those who think that because the Senate should, forsooth, use its constitutional veto and turn down legislation which has been sent to it by this House, we should therefore reform the upper chamber. I think the members of that body have as much brains, as much judgment, and as much good sense as the members of this House, and they can focus their views on any particular question with just as much acuteness and intelligence as we can. I have been at some of the Senate committee meetings occasionally and have been impressed by that fact. I say this because the Senate is spoken of sometimes as a body of old, worn out politicians. I venture that statement and I say it boldly- and it is no insult to the members of the *Commons to make the statement. In any event such a statement does not justify making constitutional changes in the Senate.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Is my hon. friend going to the Senate?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I am afraid that I will
never have the financial qualifications to get into the Senate. If there was a Senate vacancy to-day and the Prime Minister and his government should come to me at midnight and ask me to take a seat in the upper chamber unfortunately I could not do so, because I have not the necessary financial qualifications; I have too many mortgages attached to my little home. Therefore I am not looking for a Senate position for the next few years to come. However, that is by the way.
Some hon. members say we should reform the Senate because it is partisan. Do the gentlemen who advance that statement consider for a moment how they are going to render the Senate non-partisan? In British countries we have had partisan government for generation on generation, and I say on the whole we have been fairly well governed. As I said a few moments ago the British Empire has progressed under partisan government through the ages, and is to-day as great in her strength and glory as she ever was. The United States has progressed under par-

The Senate
tisan government; so have all Anglo Saxon countries. They have all made mistakes but who in this world does not err. Point me out a man who has reached maturity and who has never made any mistakes in his life, and I will show you an individual who has never accomplished anything. There is only one way to avoid criticism, it is to do nothing, to say nothing and to be nothing. Criticism is indispensable. Governments, at times, should be criticized. It is a good thing to criticize, but when an hon. member says the Senate is partisan how is he going to make it otherwise? Would the Senate be rendered less partisan by appointing a few of the followers of my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke)? They would be Progressive partisans. Would the Senate be made less partisan by appointing followers of the gentleman who leads the labour forces of this country? I presume they would be partisan also. I have only to point out to those who say we should make the Senate non-partisan that there are partisans in the upper chamber to-day and will be for many generations in the future. To have it otherwise as things are would be an impossibility. I am not blaming our farmer friends for being partisan; they must be such, their very constitution requires them to be partisan.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Narrow-minded partisans.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I do not say they are
narrow-minded partisans.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Well, of one class.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I do not say they are
of one class either. I affirm that they are just as broad-minded as the Liberals or Conservatives in this House. Still they are partisan, the very nature of the constitution to which they give their adherence, makes them partisan; and if we to-day put six representatives from each of the prairie provinces in the Senate they would be Progressive partisans, and would look out, perhaps, more for their own friends than they would for persons of the Conservative or Liberal stripe of politics. I repeat I should like to get some concrete illustration of how hon. gentlemen are going to reform' the Senate so as to make it non-partisan.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Abolish it.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: I am against the abolition of the Senate.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
asked for our opinion.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I am not finding fault
with the hon. member. However, I am against 60i
the abolition of the upper chamber upon what
appear to me to be very strong and sound grounds. The abolition of the Senate would perhaps result in greater difficulty than would be the case if the upper house were simply reformed. Another hon. gentleman states that we should abolish the Senate because it does not represent the national life of this country. That is a question which I have not studied.
I presume the Senate should represent all phases of our national life-commercial, political, religious, and all the rest. However, I do not know what the present complexion of the Senate is in these respects, I have never gone into that phase . of the matter. If such is the case it is not the fault of the constitution of the Senate but rather the fault of the persons who made the appointments to the Senate; and if the appointments were to be made in some other way I do not see that it would mend the situation in the least.
I would not have an elective Senate because if its members are partisans now they would then be twice as partisan. We have too many elections in this country at the present time under our present system, and we do not want to have any more.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
Some hon. members laugh, but I say that we are cursed with too many elections, civic, provincial and federal. I would not 'have an elective Senate; I would not amend the constitution from that viewpoint. I would have the Senate appointed as at present. I am now coming to the question of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean):	Would I reform the Senate? Very
little. I am no prophet, but I want to make a prophecy here to-night, and it is this: we will see no reform in the constitution of the Senate of this country for many years. We may have our conferences with provincial premiers and attorneys general. I am not criticizing the government for calling these conferences, because that is the first tangible step which has ever been taken in this country to arrive at a realization of what should be done towards the reform of the Senate. I prophesy to-night-it does not cost much * that when that conference meets here there will not be one concrete proposition on which the representatives of all the provinces of Canada will agree, and that will cause the breaking up of the conference.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
And of the government perhaps.
The Senate

speechtext: No. I do not think the government is bound by the result of a conference. I hear applause from the other side of the House, but I would rather have it come from this side. When I say that is all they will do, I mean that is all they are capable of doing. I hear loud applause. What little things my friends will applaud. They will not give me a chance to finish a sentence. That is all they can do or are capable of doing, in so far as this .conference is concerned.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Why not have the conference bring down its proposal first and have that constitute a basis of negotiation?
