speechtext:
I quite admit that he is
capable of doing anything.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: He cannot do anything that is impossible and to amend the constitution in vacation time is an impossibility.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: It was not amending the constitution in vacation time that was suggested. What my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Hoey) suggested was that the undertaking given last session be made the subject of a government measure now for submission later at a conference. That seems a pretty good idea. What does the hon. member think of it?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: My hon. friend has spent a long enough time in public life to know that that would be a clumsy way of doing business It would be dictation to the provincial governments, and if there is anything the provincial governments resent, it is dictation from the federal government,.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Is it any' more than a declaration of policy, without any suggestion of conference?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: The suggestion is that the conference should take place first. The first intimation given of the conference was in the Speech from the Throne.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: No. WThen the bald announcement was made I asked the Prime Minister if he had considered the matter, and asked the provinces what their -will was, and he made no reply; on the contrary he went through the western provinces and never mentioned the conference at all, but declared to the whole country that he was going to reform the Senate.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: I know the Prime Minister loves the leader of the opposition very much, but he does not love him well enough to tell him six months ahead of time what the government policy is going to be.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: I told him.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: I doubt if he would fo; low the hon. gentleman's advice.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: He has followed it-a year late.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
That is the situation as I regard this matter. I believe there should be some suspensory power in the Senate. And why? Three, four, five or six bills are sent to the Senate in the dying days of parliament. They are thrown in there. They may have passed this House with little or no debate. They are sent over to the Senate, to be dealt with in one day, or perhaps two or three days. I think that is very unfair to the the Senate. I say that in a case of that kind the Senate should have what I would call a suspensory power, and should say to the Commons, " We do not know sufficient about this particular measure to say whether we will agree to it or not. We will suspend judgment for the present session of parliament and will take the matter up next year". If they do not deal with those bills the next year or the following year, say in two years, then I say there might be, in connection with that suspensory power, the right in the House of Commons to pass those bills, so long as they obtained the signature of the King's representative in this country. I think that is a fair proposition; it would be a different matter if some important question arose which should have full, free and fair discussion, and in regard to which the Senate was aware of all the intricacies and the pros and cons of the measure. In such a case I would say they should have the suspensory power. I can well understand why the Senate of this country would be loth-and we would all be loth- to vote on a subject without knowing anything about it.

The Senate
I do not blame the Senate for their conduct in the past, because they refused to pass bills in the dyings days of the session when they could not give them fair consideration, nor will I criticize them adversely in the future for such conduct. Hon. gentlemen may tell me they have a right to remain here and give these measures consideration. Well, we know that some members in this House do not love them very much, and we know how very much less we would have loved them if, on the eighteenth day of July last, we were told by the Senate that they were going to remain in session another month to give further consideration to certain measures. I say the only solution is the suspensory power, coupled with the provision that there should be no return made of a bill suspended by the Senate unless they had taken some specific action on it, and if they failed for two years to take that specific action- there should be some power in the House of Commons, with the signature of the Governor General, to make that bill law. That is as far as I would go in any reform as far as the Senate is concerned.
I have spoken a great deal longer than I intended to owing to a great many interruptions, for which I am not criticizing my hon. friends. I think the Senate as at present constituted is a very important part of our constitution, and in looking over the political history of this country, I do not know if there is any great reason for any reform of the Senate, either the one suggested or any other reform. I do not think they are made of the stuff which on all occasions would like to be opposed to public opinion in this country all the time.
I do not see why the Houi-:e of Commons should assume an attitude of superiority and infallibility; why should we presume to say that we can never go wrong? Kings have been beheaded for having that obsession, and it is tantamount to taking up that pos.hon for this branch of parliament to say that, because it has passed a bill, in the belief that public opinion is behind it, it therefore follows that the Senate must be quite wrong if it takes a different view, and that in consequence the Senate should be reformed or put out of business or both. There is nothing faulty with the resolution of my hon. friend from West Calgary in so far as it asserts that steps should be taken to consider the reform of the Senate. Nor do I think that any hon. member in this House, whatever may be his opinion on the question of Senate reform, will vote against such a proposition. As to an}' amendment to the resolution, I must vote against the first one that has been proposed, inasmuch as it declares for the abolition of
the Senate. The amendment states in effect that in the opinion of this House it is expedient that an address be presented to the King praying that the British North America Act be amended so as to provide that the Dominion of Canada,
-should either have the power to make the Senate of Canada an elective body, or to abolish it, as might be decided by the people in a plebiscite vote to be taken at the next Dominion general election.
I am opposed to that because I am opposed to the abolition of the Senate, and I am opposed to an elective Senate for the reasons I have given. I shall therefore be obliged to vote against the amendment.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext: Is the hon. member opposed to obeying the will of the people?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
No; when the will of
the people is right I always bow to it.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
Well, the amendment
simply asks that the people be consulted in the matter.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
I am afraid that they
might go wrong in this instance and vote for the abolition of the Senate.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
Then the hon. member
would not obey the people?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
This is one of the cases
where I would think the popular will had gone astray. Hon. gentlemen should not forget that we are all part of what the hon. member is pleased to include in the term "popular will". Now, there is no popular proposal which has ever been before any government that has not had some opposition; there has never been any question that has come up in this country, never any proposal, except in trivial matters, which has not been opposed by some section or -other of the country. And surely my hon. friend will concede to an opposition,, even though it be in a marked minority, the right to consider its own opinions right. That is entirely a matter for the conference to consider. I shall vote for the amendment to the amendment because I think it is in keeping with the only course we can pursue to-day, either in the matter of amending the constitution or reforming the Senate, and that is the calling of a conference. I do not say that it will necessarily amount to very much, but I do think that the members of this House are desirous of ascertaining what is, not the -public opinion but the sound public opinion in this country on out constitution so far as it relates to the Senate.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
It would be rather amusing to fol
The Senate

low some of the arguments which have been advanced on this question if there were not other matters of very great public importance demanding the attention of parliament. We have heard a good deal during the present session about amending our constitution, and this talk is becoming so general that I do not feel like sitting in my place and allowing it to go unchallenged all the time. I question whether there has ever been a session of parliament during which so manj' hon. members have expressed dissatisfaction with the existing constitution as during the present session. I regret that this should be so. The constitution was framed by those who brought about confederation in Canada, at a very difficult period in the life of our country, and it seems to me that the mere fact that it has stood the test of time so far and so well is a great tribute to the wisdom and the foresight displayed by the Fathers of Confederation. I am inclined to think therefore that this passing wave of attack on the constitution will not amount to very much.
In the present instance I would point out how the viewpoint of some people changes according to the different positions in which they find themselves. It is apparently a very common and a favourite relaxation on the part of some when in opposition to attack the Senate and make every effort they can to concentrate the attention of the people to the institution, with a view to representing the constitution in this particular respect as being all wrong. I have heard this line of argument advanced quite often by gentlemen who were afterwards members of the upper chamber, and once they entered the sacred precincts of the Senate no more was heard of their objections to the constitution of that body as it stands.
Personally, I do not say that there are not times when the people have reason for finding some fault with the way in which the Senate is constituted; this has been the case in the past, and I suppose that occasions will arise in the future when the same thing may perhaps be felt. The method of appointment and the lack of care shown sometimes are doubtless responsible for this. I think that on the whole my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Carroll) has indicated that he does not attach very much importance to the paragraph in the Speech from the Throne relating to this question of Senate reform, nor to the resolution which was moved this afternoon by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw). And he does not anticipate that the government will take any action in the matter. So that the discussion is not going

to bring about any very great results. I think myself that the resolution might very well have been ruled out of order by reason of the fact that it is beyond the jurisdiction of this House to deal with- the matter therein suggested. But I am not going to argue that point.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond, however, touched upon a matter which I do not feel like allowing to pass without some comment. When asked about his personal ambitions, and whether he had any inclination or desire to qualify for the Senate, he replied that he had not the necessary financial qualifications for a senator-ship. Let me point out, he has the financial qualification to be elected as the representative of his constituency, and he has had those qualifications for quite a number of years. I have known the member for Cape Breton South and Richmond for a long time, and if senators are to be appointed from the different parties, I dp not know of anyone that I would rather see in the Senate from the other side of the House than my hon. friend, and I am sure that he would render good service to the country in the upper chamber, for we all admire the frankness with which he discusses public questions in this House. But for the present at least I think he will render better service where he is.
Now, I happen to have on my desk a report of a committee of the Senate. I was looking at this when the member for Cape Breton South and Richmond spoke, and I had no intention of taking part in this debate had he not referred to the financial qualifications necessary for a seat in the upper house which this report refers to. It may be remembered that some years ago there was quite a scandal about the sale of senatorships, it being charged that a price was placed upon them. Some of you may not have remembered the circumstances as I have, for the reason that the member for the constituency which I now have the honour to represent was the minister who to a certain extent was implicated. An exmember of parliament alleged that a demand had been made upon him for $10,000 for a seat in the Senate. This naturally caused a good deal of comment throughout the country and resulted in a special committee of the upper house holding an investigation, the charge being considered to be a serious reflection upon the members of the Senate. The investigation took place in 1901. I remember it very well because one of the parties implicated had also sent a letter which was read at the Liberal convention in my constituency. When the Liberal candidate was nominated,

The Senate
in which he pointed out the reason why a certain candidate who was much talked of and was likely to be selected by the Liberals should not be given the nomination, simply because he had absolutely refused to contribute funds towards running the machine, and had stated he had no money to contribute for elections and consequently he was not deemed to be a desirable man even to receive a Liberal nomination. Such things have caused a good deal of discontent and suspicion among the people with regard to appointments to the upper chamber, but fortunately we have not had any such scandal for many years. I think I might very well read some of the evidence which was taken before the special committee of the Senate on that occasion. The party who made the charge was Mr. H. H. Cook at one time Liberal member for South Simcoe, I think. He was defeated in 1896 and felt himself entitled to a senatorship by reason of his party services. With respect to Mr. Kerr's appointment to the Senate, Mr. Cook referred to the agent who had approached him in the matter and who claimed he represented the government or Sir Richard Cartwright. He was asked to tell what took place between him and the agent. He answered:
The party wrote me a letter. I was away from home at the time. The letter was written stating-
The question was objected to.
Q. Just tell the the interview, what took place.
By the Hon. Mr. Dandurand:
Q. Could you fix the date?-A. No.
Q. Or about?-A. No, it was before this appointment was made, before Mr. Kerr was appointed. He came to my office and said that he had just a short time ago come from Ottawa, and he was instructed to ask me for $10,000 for a senatorship.
By Counsel for Mr. Cook:
Q. How did he greet you?-A. When he came into my office, from the corridor, from the hall, to my outer office, he passed through the outer office, and he said, "Good morning, Mr. Cook"-or rather, "Good morning Mr. Senator." I said, "Good morning." Then he walked in and closed the door behind him and said that he had returned from Ottawa, and was instructed to ask me for $10,000 for the appointment. He told me either-I have forgotten w*hether he said the government or Sir Richard Cartwright told him to come and see me, and I told him most emphatically that I would not give him $10,000, or the government, or Sir Richard Cartwright, or anyone else, for a senatorship. "Well," he stated, "if you don't give it to me you wont get the appointment."
And he did not.
"They are very desirous of giving it to you, and want to give it to you, but they wont give it to you unless you pay them $10,000. You are able to pay it, and they want the money for party purposes." That is about the gist of the conversation, and he went out of the office.
Now the evidence which Mr. Cook gave was substantiated by the evidence of Mr. Hieland Hancock. He was sworn and examined by Mr. Ritchie, counsel for the committee, as follows:
Q. You are bookkeeper for the Ontario Lumber Corn-pay?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Of which Mr. Cook is president, I understand? -A. Yes.
Hon. Mr. Dandurand suggests that as this is a witness for the prosecution he should be examined by counsel for Mr. Cook. Mr. Ritchie, counsel for the committee, assents.
By Mr. Marsh, counsel for Mr. Cook:
Q. You remember the occasion of Mr. Preston visiting the office of Mr. Cook?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Can you tell us about what time that was?-A.
It was in the fall of 1898.
Q. Tell me what happened when he visited the office?-A. When he came into the office, as soon as he reached the door of Mr. Cook's room, he said, "Good morning, Mr. Senator."
Q. And then what happened?-A. Then he went in and closed the door.
Q. He went into Mr. Cook's private room then, and closed the door?-A. Yes.
Q. About how long were they together?-A. I should say about fifteen or twenty minutes, I would not be positive as to that.
Q. I presume you could not hear anything that took place while they were together?-A. No, sir.
Q. Then what next happened?-A. Mr. Cook and Mr. Preston came out, and Mr. Cook saw Mr. Preston to the outer door of the office.
Q. They came out of Mr. Cook's private room?- A. Yes.
Q. Through the room where you were?-A. Through the room where I was.
Q. And then what was done?-A. Mr. Cook saw Mr. Preston out.
Q. Out of the door?-A. Out of the outer door.
Q. Then what happened?-A. Mr. Cook came back to the desk where I was, and seemed very indignant- Mr. Blake, counsel for the accused parties, objects to this evidence. Objection overruled.
Q. You say that when Mr. Cook took Mr. Preston to the door, immediately upon closing the door Mr. Cook returned to you. In what frame of mind was he or what condition did he appear to be in?-A. He appeared to be very angry.
Q. And what did he say?-A. He said to me, "What do you think of that damned scoundrel Preston?"
Q. And then what happened?-A. I said, "What is the matter Mr. Cook?" He said, "He wanted me to pay $10,000 for a senatorship."
Q. Anything further?-A. Nothing further.
And so on. Now, this was one Mr. W. T. R. Preston, at the time of this investigation immigration agent over in England, brought back to give evidence at this inquiry; formerly organizer for the Liberal party; librarian at the parliament buildings, Toronto, at the time of the famous election episodes throughout, this province; the man who was responsible for raising the funds to grease the machine; the man who sent the famous telegram to Donald McNish the night of the election in West Elgin in 1899 to hug the members of the much abused threshing machine for the days of auld lang syne. Fortunately there was an end to the regime of those years, and a general clean-up took place in 1905. Mr. Blake, who was counsel at that time for the accused, was the man who came out and denounced more vigorously than anyone else in the Liberal party the things that had been done
The Senate

by those whose names I mentioned in a previous debate and the members of the machine. Fortunately for the public life of this country and for the reputation of the people of this Dominion we have not lately had much of that sort of thing to contend -with. I had hoped that we would hear nothing further with regard to those who were connected with these events of about a quarter of a century ago, but I regret very much indeed that there is considerable evidence to-day of their activities in the public life of this country.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT AND CONSTITUTION-RESOLUTION PROPOSED BY MR. SHAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
however interesting the remarks of the last speaker (Mr. Sutherland) may be to certain members in this House, they do not pertain very directly, I think, to the resolution under consideration.
I have sometimes wondered whether the Canadian Senate might be described as a comedy or as a tragedy. In fact, I sometimes wonder whether this House is a comedy or a tragedy. I remember a few years ago being told by a friend of mine who was rather prominently connected with the farmers' movement in Ontario that he had been offered a senatorship. I do not think he spent two seconds in deciding what to do, and I should have decided the same as he did'; because if he had ever consented to accept a senator-ship under the existing conditions he would have been everlastingly condemned by the farmers of Ontario. There is no doubt that the farmers of Ontario, generally speaking, are strongly in favour of the abolition of the Senate. I would suggest to the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll)-I am sorry he is not in his seat,- that there is another motto different from the one which his speech exemplified, namely that "the wish is father to the thought." There is another motto, I say, that he ought to keep in mind and it is "Where there's a will there's a way." He has magnified the difficulties before us in the way of Senate reform. I am free to admit the difficulties; we face difficulties wherever we turn. But I should like to commend to him and to the House that old motto, "Where there's a will there's a way." In regard to the point raised by the last speaker, I too, heard some years ago about the purchase of senatorships. I hope that is something of the past. But there is no doubt in my mind that the evidence which was presented and the tales that were told some years ago have helped to bring our Senate into disrepute. The views that are current regarding our Senate are very well exemplified in the following clipping from the Victoria Times:

The Canadian Senate is the most reactionary legislative body in the English-speaking world. There is no other institution with such far-reaching powers in any British Dominion. It would not be tolerated in Britain, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, and the fact that in its present form it has been tolerated so long in Canada is not a healthy symptom in our people. It should be made more responsive to those who pay for its maintenance and whose will it ought to carry out. Its members should have to give an account of their stewardship to the electors from time to time, if for no other reason than to remind them that they are the servants and not the masters of the public. If this were done the Senate would cease to be the trump card of small but powerful elements who for selfish purposes desire the rejection of legislation affecting them which has been passed by the House of Commons.
Whether right or wrong, that is the situation that faces us; that is the opinion that prevails very largely throughout this country and it is something which we shall have to reckon with.
I hold in my hand a rather interesting document which has been referred to by a former speaker, A Political Cathechism, written by T. A. Patrick, who, I understand, is a resident of the province of Saskatchewan. Let me quote Just a few sentences from this document, which I presume has been sent to all members of the House:
Q. Who other than senators are opposed to real Senate reform?-A. Every actual or prospective political derelict, lacking sad, ballast, or cargo, fearful of foundering, is eager to be taken in tow. Every political jobber who values the Senate patronage for the support it will buy; every sectional interest, and every selfish interest that thrives best on unfair advantage and special privilege.
Such is another expression of public opinion in regard to this matter, and in spite of all difficulties, whether public opinion is right or wrong, it is going to make itself felt pretty soon in one form or another. I should like further to direct the attention of the House [DOT]to something which I think is also partly responsible for the formation of public opinion in regard to the Senate. I have in my hand a clipping from the Farmers' Sun of 1922-
I have not the exact date of it, but it is some time during that year. It contains a copy of a letter sent out by a certain W. O. Sealey, of Hamilton, who was at that time striving for a senatorship. This letter is quite worth while placing on Hansard. I read:
Hamilton, Ont., March 8, 1922.
Dear Sir:
Owing to the death of the late Senator Milne, the Hamilton senatorship is now vacant.
Having been a continuous worker and supporter of the Liberal party for the past forty years, a candidate in five campaigns for the Dominion parliament, necessitating the expenditure of the greater part of my time, I acquired a good parliamentary experience, and our continued success seemed assured until we were defeated with the government in 1911.

The Senate
My political merits appear to be most worthy, and at least a good average for the whole province.
I am now a candidate for the Senate vacancy, so if my comparison of merit appeals to you as being about correct, then I wish you would be kind enough to write the Premier, Hon. Mackenzie King, Parliament Building, Ottawa, (as well as any other Ontario member of the cabinet you may know), immediately, recommending and urging my appointment, believing that if honoured with the appointment, I could still continue to be very useful to the party and community-
Party first, of course.
-as most people feel I was during my parliamentary career-
I do not quite understand him, Mr. Speaker, when he refers to his parliamentary career. I presume it was his participation in five campaigns. I continue:
If by chance you don't find the time or convenience to write quickly, and the enclosed draft letter expresses your sentiments, then kindly date, sign and mail at once and much oblige.
Our Wentworth candidate, Mr. W. T. Evans, suggested that he would be glad to have the views of the Liberal friends of Wentworth on matters of patronage or appointments, so if the enclosed card expresses your views, kindly date, sign and mail same.
Thanking you in anticipation for your immediate attention to the above, and with best wishes as usual.
Yours truly,
W. O. Sealey.
And enclosed there are very eloquent appeals to the Prime Minister and to Mr. Evans on behalf of Mr. Sealey, so as to save the recipient the labour of composing a letter of his own. I shall not read them, as it is not necessary.

I suppose this is comedy in a sense, but after all, from the standpoint of the country's welfare, it is very tragic; and if I may be allowed to say so, I think it is a very serious reflection upon the party system. I do not wish to speak at any length in regard to the matter under discussion. I should like, in conclusion, to refer to the resolution, the amendment, and the subamendment that have been moved. The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) moves in amendment to the said amendment:
That all the words after the word "That" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:

Now when, this subamendment was moved I thought it might have reference to the first "that" in the first line of the resolution, but I think, however, that the meaning is, and it
The Senate

ought to be, that the reference is to the second "that", namely, the word "that" in the first line of the specific amendment. If that is the meaning, which I take it to be, the subamendment will read as follows:

Therefore it is expedient that the House approves of the convening at an early date of a conference between the government of the Dominion of Canada and the governments of the various provinces to consider the advisability of amending the British North America Act with respect to the constitution and the powers of the Senate.
That, I take it, is thei motion as sought to be amended by the hon. member for Joliette. If that is the correct interpretation, I would like to say that I shall support the subamendment heartily. I am prepared to go further than the negative resolution. If the subamendment is carried it will include the original motion. If it is defeated, then we shall have to vote on the amendment. I intend to vote against the amendment, not because I am not in sympathy with its purpose, but because I think that at this juncture it is the wrong way of tackling the problem, and I therefore feel compelled to vote against it. speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, I rise to the point of order that the amendment is void for ambiguity and inconclusiveness. The last speaker (Mr. Good) has made reference to the fact that the word "that" referred to in quotation marks in the subamendment may be the first "that" or the second "that" in the amendment. He seems to assume it is the second, but the House has no right to refer to anything but the words of the resolution in determining its validity and its order. One member might vote for the resolution on the assumption that the word "that" in quotation marks was the first "that" in the amendment; another on the assumption that it was the second. The resolution has a different meaning altogether according as one assumes it to be the first or the second. Nor can the effect be cured by any statement of intention on the part of the mover. It can only be cured by amendment, and an amendment now cannot be made. I think I have made my point clear. There is nothing more clearly established than that any motion that is ambiguous as to meaning, which may mean one thing or may mean another, which has not stated its purport altogether cannot be under consideration in this House. I am free to admit that if the subamendment had read so as to make
[Mr. Good,!
it clear that the quoted "that" was the second "that" in the amendment, it would be an amendment perfectly in order. Therefore I say it is void for ambiguity and inconclusiveness.

would find no difficulty in understanding exactly what the amendment means. I also would submit that a rule of construction of statutes is applicable to the rules of this House, namely, that you are to construe a statute in order that it may have a meaning rather than that it should not have a meaning ; and I think that you are to construe the resolution in such a way that the amendment will fit into it, rather than in a manner in which the endeavour is to make the amendment a misfit to the resolution. Therefore it is expedient that a humble address be presented to His Majesty-

That is the expression of opinion that it is desired the House should give. Both amendments are true amendments in the sense that they add something to the original motion. Two members have proposed that the expression

The Senate

Therefore it is expedient that the House approves of the convening at an early date of a conference-
The meaning is perfectly clear, it could not be clearer, but the English is not as well expressed as in the first motion. As the hon. member intended, his resolution would probably have read as follows:

Which "that" is to be taken into consideration at the present moment? Clearly the one in the amendment. The hon. member for Joliette, mark well, states "all the words after the word 'that' in the amendment." The first "that" is in the formula preceding the amendment, but the essential " that " is in the main body of the amendment. The hon. member says quite logically that all the words after the word " that " in the amendment should be struck out. Having that in mind, how will the amendment to the amendment read if accepted by the House? It becomes the main motion amended and reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Senate as at present appointed and constituted is not of the greatest advantage to Canada; therefore it is expedient that the House approve of the convening at an early date of a conference between the government of the Dominion of Canada and the government of the various provinces to consider the advisability of amending the British North America Act in respect of the constitution and the powers of the Senate.
It seems to me that it reads very clearly and very intelligibly. It is true that the hon. member for Joliette might perhaps have omitted the words "it is expedient", but I am sure the right hon. member (Mr. Meighen) does not think that this is more than a technical objection. At most, it is surplusage in the phraseology and quite easy to understand in the case of an hon. member who does not use the English language as his mother tongue. A mere surplusage does not render the amendment unintelligible.
The amendment is on the contrary quite intelligible. If the word "that" applied to the formula preceding the amendment I would agree with the right hon. gentleman and I would rule the motion out of order; but with ordinary common sense I must accept the second "that" and thus construed, the amendment is intelligible. My ruling is that the amendment is in order. There are three principles put in concrete form before the House; the main motion which sweeps away the Senate as appointed and constituted; the second principle indicates the procedure which ought to be followed to reform the Senate; that is to say, by an amendment to the British North America Act; the third principle put forward by the hon. member for Joliette favours the calling together of a conference of the governments of the Dominion and of the various provinces to deal with the issue. That is my understanding of the three questions before the House.

The Senate
The question is on the amendment to the amendment.

I want to call the
attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to a file of correspondence tabled this afternoon. The correspondence is manifestly incomplete as filed. For example there is a letter from myself to Dr. Magill, but the reply of Dr. Magill does not appear. There was also some further correspondence subsequent to that. I am sure this correspondence is on file in the department.
